Build the smallest complete Loop Engineering system: a deterministic simulator that observes state, makes a decision, performs an action, verifies the outcome, records evidence, and feeds the result back into the next iteration.

Why this project exists

This establishes the portfolio pattern used by every later level: explicit state, explicit transitions, measurable outcomes, reproducible failures, and evidence that explains why the system behaved as it did.

Builds on the previous level

Nothing. This is the reference architecture that every later project extends.

Architecture flow: Scenario → State Observer → Decision → Action → Verifier → Evidence Store → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • state-machine modeling
  • canonical event schemas
  • transition invariants
  • feedback-signal design
  • deterministic replay
  • failure injection
  • termination rules
  • latency measurement
  • success-rate metrics
  • trace inspection
  • benchmark design
  • architecture communication

Recommended implementation stack

Python, FastAPI or Streamlit, SQLite/JSONL, pytest, OpenTelemetry-style events

Build sequence

1 · Model

Define states, transitions, invariants, termination rules, and a canonical event envelope.

2 · Simulate

Implement success, retry, verifier-reject, timeout, and terminal-failure paths.

3 · Instrument

Emit structured events for observation, decision, action, verification, feedback, and termination.

4 · Break

Inject stale observations, false positives, failed actions, loops, and malformed events.

5 · Measure

Compare success rate, iterations-to-success, failure class, latency, and cost proxy.

6 · Package

Ship code, architecture, replayable traces, tests, failure matrix, benchmark table, and demo.

Definition of done

  • Every state transition is explicit and inspectable.
  • Five or more failure scenarios are reproducible from fixtures.
  • A run can be replayed from its event log.
  • The verifier can reject a plausible-looking but incorrect result.
  • The report explains why each run terminated.
  • The README contains an architecture and failure model.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • source + tests
  • architecture diagram
  • event schema
  • replay traces
  • failure matrix
  • benchmark table
  • 3-minute demo
  • engineering decision record

Public artifact

`loop-observatory`: one-command simulator plus trace viewer and reproducible failure fixtures.

Project-specific failure to avoid

A polished UI with no state model, no replay, and no measurable evidence.

Loop Engineering is the discipline of designing systems — prompts, agents, or full pipelines — that improve through repeated cycles of action, evaluation, and refinement, rather than relying on a single-shot output. Instead of asking a model to produce a perfect answer on the first try, you design a loop: generate, check the result against some signal of quality, and refine until that signal is satisfied or a budget runs out.

Why it matters

Single-shot LLM outputs plateau in reliability. Loops convert a static text predictor into a system capable of self-correction, multi-step problem solving, and adaptation — trading extra compute and latency for meaningfully higher reliability.

Core concepts

  • The generate → evaluate → refine cycle
  • Convergence vs. divergence of iterative refinement
  • Loop termination conditions and stopping rules
  • Feedback signal design (what tells the loop "good enough"?)

Real-world example

A coding agent writes a function, runs the test suite, reads the failures, and rewrites the function — repeating this cycle until the tests pass or an attempt budget is exhausted.

Common mistake

Treating "add a loop" as a universal fix. A loop without a well-defined stopping condition or a trustworthy quality signal just repeats — or amplifies — the same mistake instead of correcting it.

Further reading

  • Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models" (2022)
  • Shinn et al., "Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning" (2023)

Iterative, feedback-driven design is far older than language models. It traces from control theory and Norbert Wiener's cybernetics (1948), through reinforcement learning's trial-and-error optimization, through software engineering's CI/CD pipelines and Agile sprints as human-operated loops, to the 2022–2024 wave of LLM agent loops (ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT-style systems) that automated the observe–correct cycle inside the model's own reasoning.

Why it matters

Understanding this lineage clarifies that agent loops aren't a novel invention — they're the application of decades-old control and optimization theory to language models, which means many of their hard problems (stability, termination, reward shaping) already have a body of prior work to draw on.

Core concepts

  • Cybernetics and the feedback loop
  • Reinforcement learning's trial-and-error optimization
  • DevOps CI/CD as a human-operated loop
  • The emergence of LLM-driven autonomous loops

Real-world example

A CI/CD pipeline — build, test, deploy, monitor, fix — is a loop operated by humans and tooling together. ReAct-style agents automate the same shape almost entirely in text.

Common mistake

Assuming "loop engineering" started with GPT-based agents in 2022–23, and ignoring the control-systems and RL heritage that supplies most of the theory behind stable, convergent loops.

Further reading

  • Norbert Wiener, "Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine" (1948)
  • Sutton & Barto, "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction"

Loops convert LLMs from static text predictors into systems capable of self-correction, multi-step problem solving, and adaptation to environments they weren't explicitly trained on. They matter most exactly where a task's full solution can't be planned correctly in one shot.

Why it matters

Error correction beats first-try accuracy at scale. Loops trade extra compute and latency for reliability — a trade that's worth making for long-horizon coding, research, and other multi-step agentic tasks.

Core concepts

  • First-try accuracy vs. loop-corrected accuracy
  • Compute/latency cost as the price of reliability
  • Long-horizon tasks that require multi-step correction

Real-world example

Customer support agents that fail silently on a first attempt but succeed after a self-critique-and-retry loop; code agents like Claude Code iterating edit → test → fix until green.

Common mistake

Over-looping: adding retries without bounding cost or latency, which causes runaway compute or endless refinement that never actually converges.

Further reading

  • METR's evaluations of AI agentic task-horizon length
  • Anthropic and OpenAI engineering posts on tool-use loop design

Loop-based systems now run across software engineering (coding agents, CI/CD), customer support, research (literature review and hypothesis refinement), finance (strategy backtesting), robotics (sense–plan–act), content moderation (review and appeal), and healthcare (diagnosis-support pipelines with human oversight).

Why it matters

Each domain shapes its loop differently based on the cost of a wrong iteration — recognizing that shape is the difference between a loop that helps and one that quietly causes harm.

Core concepts

  • Domain-specific loop shapes
  • Human-in-the-loop vs. fully autonomous loops
  • Closed-loop vs. open-loop systems

Real-world example

Claude Code's plan → edit → test → review loop for software; iterative structure-refinement loops in protein-folding systems like AlphaFold.

Common mistake

Applying the same loop shape to every domain regardless of the cost of a wrong iteration — a diagnosis-support loop needs human gating; a code-lint loop usually doesn't.

Further reading

  • Documentation and case studies from agent frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen)
  • Industry reports on agentic AI adoption by sector

The frontier is moving toward agent societies (multiple specialized loops coordinating), tighter integration of evaluation loops into training itself (RLHF/RLAIF as a meta-loop), standardized loop protocols for tool use, and systems that rewrite their own prompts or strategies.

Why it matters

Knowing where the field is heading helps you design loops today that won't need a rebuild tomorrow — favoring composable, protocol-friendly loop designs over bespoke ones.

Core concepts

  • Recursive self-improvement
  • Test-time compute scaling
  • Meta-learning loops (loops that tune other loops)

Real-world example

Extended-thinking models that run internal reasoning loops at inference time, rather than relying solely on loops built at training time.

Common mistake

Assuming more loop iterations always mean better outcomes — returns diminish and can turn negative as cost scales with iteration count, which is why the field is optimizing for smarter loops, not just more of them.

Further reading

  • Research on test-time compute scaling laws
  • Papers on self-refine and self-consistency prompting

Four mental models do most of the work in loop design: the OODA loop (Observe–Orient–Decide–Act) from military strategy; the Generate–Evaluate–Refine cycle as the minimal loop unit; the thermostat model (sensor, comparator, actuator) from control theory; and the "loop budget" — every loop has a finite compute, time, or attempt budget that shapes its design.

Why it matters

These models give you a vocabulary to diagnose a broken loop quickly: is the sensor (evaluator) untrustworthy, is the actuator (refinement step) too weak, or is the budget wrong?

Core concepts

  • OODA loop
  • Generate → Evaluate → Refine (GER)
  • Control-loop / thermostat model
  • Loop budget as a design constraint

Real-world example

Thinking of a code-review loop as a thermostat: the "sensor" is the test suite's output, the "comparator" is a pass/fail threshold, and the "actuator" is the code edit it triggers.

Common mistake

Designing a loop before deciding its budget and termination rule — leading to loops that quit too early or never converge.

Further reading

  • John Boyd's writings on the OODA loop
  • Donella Meadows, "Thinking in Systems: A Primer"

Five beliefs cause most loop-design failures: "loops always improve output" (false without a trustworthy evaluator); "more iterations are always better" (returns diminish and can go negative); "agent loops are new" (they build on decades of control theory and RL); "a loop needs a human to be safe" (some autonomous loops are safe with reversible actions and a trustworthy evaluator; others genuinely need gating); and "self-reflection fixes everything" (a model reflecting on its own output shares its own blind spots unless paired with external verification).

Why it matters

Each misconception leads to a specific, avoidable failure mode — from silent quality regressions to runaway compute spend to false confidence in "self-checked" outputs.

Core concepts

  • Evaluator quality as the true bottleneck
  • Diminishing and negative returns on iteration
  • External vs. internal verification

Real-world example

A model "reflecting" on its own faulty math without an external tool (a calculator) often just re-confirms the same wrong answer with more confidence.

Common mistake

Treating a model's self-critique as equivalent to independent, external verification, when the two catch very different classes of error.

Further reading

  • Huang et al., "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet" (2023)

Foundations

The concepts every loop is built from, now extended into modern context engineering: iteration, feedback, optimization, control, state, planning, reasoning, search, and the deliberate construction of the information boundary every model action receives.

Extend the L0 loop with a context compiler that selects task state, retrieved knowledge, recent observations, constraints, and compacted history under a hard budget and provenance policy.

Why this project exists

Context is now an engineering surface, not a prompt-writing trick. The project proves that you can measure which context improves outcomes and reject stale, conflicting, oversized, or poisoned context.

Builds on the previous level

Extends L0 event logging, verifier semantics, replay fixtures, and benchmark harness.

Architecture flow: Task + State → Context Compiler → Policy Filter → Working Context → Agent → Context Evidence → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • context contracts
  • token budgeting
  • retrieval ranking
  • recency weighting
  • authority scoring
  • context compaction
  • provenance tagging
  • conflict resolution
  • context poisoning defense
  • snapshotting
  • ablation testing
  • context-quality metrics

Recommended implementation stack

Python, Pydantic, Postgres/SQLite, vector or hybrid search, LLM API, OpenTelemetry/logging

Build sequence

1 · Contract

Define allowed context fields, token budget, source authority, freshness, sensitivity, and provenance.

2 · Assemble

Combine task state, recent events, retrieved facts, constraints, and summaries into typed sections.

3 · Select

Rank by relevance, recency, authority, uncertainty, and cost; enforce hard limits.

4 · Compact

Compress old history while preserving decisions, unresolved items, provenance, and invariants.

5 · Attack + Evaluate

Run stale, noisy, poisoned, contradictory, and budget-pressure ablations against L0 baselines.

6 · Package

Publish context traces, token/cost analysis, ablation report, failure cases, and demo.

Definition of done

  • Context budget is enforced in code.
  • Every retrieved item has provenance and freshness metadata.
  • Stale or conflicting context triggers a defined policy.
  • Ablation tests quantify the contribution of each context source.
  • The L0 verifier still works with the new context layer.
  • Context snapshots can be replayed.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • context snapshots
  • token/cost report
  • ablation study
  • provenance examples
  • poisoning test
  • before/after benchmark
  • demo
  • design note

Public artifact

`context-engineering-lab`: reproducible context compiler with traces and ablation runner.

Project-specific failure to avoid

Stuffing more text into prompts without measuring context quality or budget effects.

LangChain’s 2026 survey identifies quality as a top production barrier while observability is already widespread; this project makes context quality measurable rather than anecdotal.

Iteration is the act of repeating a process, each time using the output of the previous pass as input to the next. In loop engineering it's the mechanical backbone: every loop is, at minimum, "do the thing again, differently."

Why it matters

Without a clear model of what changes between iterations — the input, the strategy, the context — a loop degenerates into just repeating the same failed attempt.

Core concepts

  • Fixed-point iteration (repeating until output stops changing)
  • Iteration variable — what specifically changes each pass
  • Bounded vs. unbounded iteration

Real-world example

A prompt-refinement loop that appends the previous failure reason to the next prompt, so each pass has strictly more information than the last.

Common mistake

Re-running the same prompt or plan verbatim and hoping for a different result, instead of changing something informed by the prior attempt's outcome.

Further reading

  • Classic numerical methods texts on fixed-point iteration

A feedback system feeds a portion of a process's output back in as input, so the system can respond to its own results. Negative feedback pushes the system toward a target (correcting error); positive feedback amplifies deviation (useful for growth, dangerous for stability).

Why it matters

Nearly every "loop" in loop engineering is really a feedback system in disguise — distinguishing negative from positive feedback tells you whether a loop will stabilize or blow up.

Core concepts

  • Negative feedback (error-correcting)
  • Positive feedback (amplifying)
  • Feedback delay and its effect on stability
  • Signal-to-noise ratio in the feedback channel

Real-world example

A self-critique loop where the model's own confidence score feeds back as a stopping signal — negative feedback if confidence rises with correctness, runaway if it doesn't.

Common mistake

Building a feedback loop without checking whether the signal is actually correlated with the thing you want to improve — a noisy or misleading signal makes the loop worse than none.

Further reading

  • Norbert Wiener, "Cybernetics" (1948)

Optimization is the search for the best solution according to some objective, typically by iteratively adjusting a candidate solution to improve that objective. Loop engineering borrows its core vocabulary — objective functions, local optima, gradient signals — directly from optimization theory.

Why it matters

An agent loop is an optimization process even when no math is involved: each iteration is a step intended to move the output closer to some target, and it can get stuck in local optima just like gradient descent can.

Core concepts

  • Objective functions
  • Local vs. global optima
  • Exploration vs. exploitation trade-off
  • Convergence criteria

Real-world example

A prompt-optimization loop that keeps refining wording toward higher scores on a held-out evaluation set — and can get stuck over-fitting to that specific evaluation set (a local optimum) rather than generalizing.

Common mistake

Optimizing a proxy objective (e.g., "length of output") that's easy to measure instead of the real objective (e.g., "usefulness"), which quietly degrades what you actually care about.

Further reading

  • Boyd & Vandenberghe, "Convex Optimization"

A control system continuously measures a process's actual state, compares it to a desired setpoint, and adjusts inputs to close the gap. The classic PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) controller reacts to the current error, its accumulated history, and its rate of change.

Why it matters

PID's three terms map directly onto agent-loop design questions: react to the current gap (P), don't ignore persistent small errors (I), and don't overshoot by reacting too aggressively to fast changes (D).

Core concepts

  • Setpoint and error signal
  • Proportional, integral, derivative response
  • Overshoot and oscillation
  • Stability margins

Real-world example

An agent that scales how aggressively it rewrites a plan based on how far off-track it currently is (proportional), while also tracking whether it's been stuck for several turns running (integral).

Common mistake

Reacting only to the current error and ignoring accumulated history, which causes a loop to repeatedly almost-converge without ever fully closing small persistent gaps.

Further reading

  • Åström & Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers"

A state machine models a system as a finite set of states plus the rules that transition it from one state to another in response to events. Loop engineering uses state machines to make an agent's behavior explicit and debuggable, rather than an implicit tangle of conditionals.

Why it matters

Naming an agent loop's states (e.g., "planning," "executing," "reviewing," "done") turns an opaque loop into something you can log, visualize, and reason about transition-by-transition.

Core concepts

  • States, transitions, and events
  • Entry/exit actions per state
  • Illegal-transition handling

Real-world example

A coding agent modeled with explicit states — Plan → Edit → Test → (pass: Review, fail: Edit) → Done — makes it obvious exactly where a stuck loop is stuck.

Common mistake

Leaving loop state implicit in scattered variables and prompt history instead of an explicit model, which makes failures nearly impossible to diagnose after the fact.

Further reading

  • Harel, "Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems" (1987)

Finite automata are the formal, mathematical version of state machines — a precise model (states, alphabet, transition function, start state, accepting states) used in computer science to reason rigorously about what a system can and can't do. Deterministic (DFA) and nondeterministic (NFA) variants differ in whether each state has exactly one valid next transition per input.

Why it matters

Thinking of an agent loop's control flow as a formal automaton lets you ask provable questions — is every state reachable? Can the loop get stuck in a state with no valid exit? — rather than only testing empirically.

Core concepts

  • States, alphabet, transition function
  • Deterministic vs. nondeterministic automata
  • Accepting states and reachability

Real-world example

Modeling an agent's tool-use protocol as a DFA to formally verify that no sequence of tool calls can leave the agent in an undefined or unhandled state.

Common mistake

Adding new states to a loop ad hoc as edge cases appear, instead of periodically re-verifying the whole automaton stays well-defined and terminating.

Further reading

  • Hopcroft, Motwani & Ullman, "Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation"

Planning is the process of decomposing a goal into an ordered sequence of actions before — or interleaved with — execution. In loop engineering, planning is what turns "keep trying things" into "try things in an order that's likely to work."

Why it matters

A loop with no planning step re-derives its whole approach from scratch every iteration; a loop with an explicit plan can adjust just the failing step instead of restarting.

Core concepts

  • Goal decomposition into sub-goals
  • Plan-and-execute vs. interleaved planning
  • Re-planning after a failed step

Real-world example

A research agent that first plans "search → read top 3 sources → synthesize → cite," then re-plans only the "search" step if the first pass turns up irrelevant sources.

Common mistake

Re-planning the entire task from scratch after any single step fails, which wastes the useful parts of the original plan and makes loops far slower to converge.

Further reading

  • Ghallab, Nau & Traverso, "Automated Planning and Acting"

Reasoning is the step-by-step derivation of conclusions from premises — deductive (certain, rule-based), inductive (generalizing from examples), or abductive (inferring the best explanation). Loop engineering leans heavily on reasoning as the "evaluate" half of generate-evaluate-refine.

Why it matters

The quality of a loop's refinement step is bounded by the quality of its reasoning about what went wrong — better reasoning means more targeted, effective refinements.

Core concepts

  • Deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning
  • Chain-of-thought as externalized reasoning
  • Reasoning errors vs. knowledge errors

Real-world example

An agent that reasons abductively about a test failure — "the most likely explanation for this stack trace is an off-by-one error in the loop bound" — rather than randomly trying edits.

Common mistake

Confusing a knowledge gap (the model doesn't know a fact) with a reasoning failure (the model has the facts but combines them wrong) — the fixes for each are completely different.

Further reading

  • Wei et al., "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (2022)

Search is the systematic exploration of a space of possible solutions or action sequences, typically depicted as a tree or graph. Breadth-first, depth-first, best-first, and Monte Carlo approaches trade off completeness, optimality, and cost differently.

Why it matters

Many "agent loops" are secretly search: Tree-of-Thoughts and Graph-of-Thoughts are explicit search over reasoning paths, and even simple retry loops are a degenerate one-branch search.

Core concepts

  • Search tree / graph representation
  • Breadth-first vs. depth-first vs. best-first search
  • Heuristics and pruning
  • Monte Carlo Tree Search

Real-world example

A Tree-of-Thoughts agent that explores several candidate reasoning branches in parallel, scores each with a heuristic, and prunes the weakest before continuing — rather than committing to one linear chain.

Common mistake

Running an unbounded search over reasoning paths without a pruning heuristic, which multiplies cost combinatorially for only marginal quality gains.

Further reading

  • Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (2023)
  • Russell & Norvig, "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach" (search chapters)

Decision making is the step where an agent commits to one action among several candidates, typically by scoring each option against an objective and picking the best-scoring one — or sampling probabilistically among the top options.

Why it matters

A loop's refine step is only as good as its decision procedure: generating good candidates is wasted if the selection step picks poorly among them.

Core concepts

  • Scoring and ranking candidate actions
  • Greedy vs. probabilistic selection
  • Multi-criteria decision making

Real-world example

A code-review agent that generates three candidate fixes, scores each against "tests pass" and "diff size," and picks the smallest diff that still passes.

Common mistake

Always picking the single top-scoring candidate greedily, which can trap a loop in a locally-good-but-globally-poor path when a slightly lower-scored option would have opened better options downstream.

Further reading

  • Russell & Norvig, "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach" (decision theory chapters)

An objective is the explicit statement of what "better" means for a given loop — the yardstick every evaluation step measures against. Without one, "improve" has no direction.

Why it matters

A vague objective ("make it good") can't drive a loop; a precise, measurable objective ("all unit tests pass and cyclomatic complexity doesn't increase") can.

Core concepts

  • Explicit vs. implicit objectives
  • Single-objective vs. multi-objective design
  • Objective misspecification

Real-world example

A writing-refinement loop with the explicit objective "reduce word count by 20% while preserving every factual claim" gives the refine step a concrete target to hit.

Common mistake

Leaving the objective implicit in a vague instruction, which forces the evaluator to guess at intent and produces inconsistent judgments across iterations.

Further reading

  • Literature on Goodhart's Law and objective misspecification

A reward function is a numeric, computable version of an objective — the formalization reinforcement learning uses to score actions and outcomes. In loop engineering, reward functions are what turn "the evaluator liked this" into a gradient a system can actually optimize against.

Why it matters

A poorly shaped reward function is the single most common cause of loops that technically converge but toward the wrong thing — the system optimizes exactly what you measured, not what you meant.

Core concepts

  • Reward shaping
  • Sparse vs. dense rewards
  • Reward hacking

Real-world example

An agent rewarded for "shorter conversations" that learns to end conversations prematurely rather than resolve issues faster — reward hacking the letter of the metric.

Common mistake

Using a single sparse end-of-task reward for a long-horizon loop, which gives almost no signal about which of many intermediate steps actually helped.

Further reading

  • Amodei et al., "Concrete Problems in AI Safety" (2016) — reward hacking section

Memory is whatever a loop carries forward from one iteration to the next — beyond just the immediate output. It's the difference between a loop that treats each pass independently and one that accumulates understanding over time.

Why it matters

Without memory, a loop can repeat the exact mistake it already diagnosed two iterations ago, because nothing persisted that diagnosis forward.

Core concepts

  • What persists across iterations vs. what resets
  • Memory as a scarce, curated resource, not a full transcript
  • Preview only — full treatment in Level 4

Real-world example

A debugging loop that keeps a running list of "approaches already tried and why they failed," so it never proposes the same fix twice.

Common mistake

Passing the entire raw iteration history forward every time instead of a curated summary — this bloats context and actually degrades the model's ability to focus on what matters.

Further reading

  • See Level 4 — Memory Loops for the full treatment

Context is everything visible to the model at the moment it acts — instructions, history, retrieved documents, tool outputs. In a loop, context is rebuilt (or edited) every iteration, and what you choose to include or drop directly shapes what the next iteration can do.

Why it matters

Context has a hard size limit and a soft attention limit — even where it technically fits, too much irrelevant context can crowd out the details that actually matter for this iteration.

Core concepts

  • Context window as a finite, shared resource
  • Context compression and summarization
  • Relevance-based context selection

Real-world example

A long research loop that summarizes earlier findings into a running brief rather than re-including every raw source document in every subsequent iteration.

Common mistake

Letting context grow unboundedly across iterations "just in case it's useful," which increases cost and can measurably degrade output quality well before the hard size limit is hit.

Further reading

  • Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts" (2023)

Error correction is the loop's actual repair mechanism: once a mistake is detected, what specifically changes to fix it. This is distinct from detection (evaluation) — correction is the action taken in response.

Why it matters

Detecting an error without a targeted correction strategy just produces an agent that knows something is wrong but doesn't reliably fix it — correction quality is what actually closes the loop.

Core concepts

  • Targeted vs. wholesale correction
  • Root-cause correction vs. symptom patching
  • Regression risk from a correction step

Real-world example

A coding agent that, on a failing test, edits only the specific function implicated by the stack trace rather than rewriting the whole file from scratch.

Common mistake

Patching the symptom shown by the evaluator (e.g., silencing a specific failing assertion) instead of the underlying root cause, which tends to resurface the same bug elsewhere.

Further reading

  • Classic software-engineering literature on root-cause analysis (e.g., the "5 Whys" technique)

Evaluation is the loop's sensor: the step that measures a candidate output against the objective and produces a signal the loop can act on — pass/fail, a score, or structured feedback. It's the single highest-leverage component in most loops, and the one most often under-built.

Why it matters

A loop cannot be more reliable than its evaluator — every other component (planning, correction, memory) is only as useful as the signal telling it whether it's on track.

Core concepts

  • Automatic vs. human vs. LLM-as-judge evaluation
  • Binary vs. graded vs. structured feedback
  • Evaluator reliability and bias

Real-world example

A code loop that trusts a real test suite's pass/fail result over a model's own self-assessment of whether the code "looks correct" — an external, ground-truth evaluator.

Common mistake

Under-investing in the evaluator relative to the generator — teams often spend far more effort making outputs better than making judgments of quality trustworthy.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Evaluation Loops for the full treatment

Reflection is a model examining its own prior output or reasoning and generating a critique of it, in natural language, before the next attempt. It's the mechanism behind Reflexion- style agents and most "self-critique" loop designs.

Why it matters

Reflection can catch a meaningful class of errors cheaply (no extra tools needed) — but, as covered in Level 0's misconceptions, it shares the same blind spots as the original generation unless paired with external checks.

Core concepts

  • Self-critique vs. externally-verified critique
  • Verbal reinforcement (Reflexion-style memory of past critiques)
  • Reflection's blind-spot problem

Real-world example

A Reflexion-style agent that, after a failed attempt, writes a short natural-language note on what went wrong and carries that note into its next attempt as extra context.

Common mistake

Relying on reflection alone for domains with objectively checkable answers (math, code) where a cheap external verifier would catch far more errors than self-critique alone.

Further reading

  • Shinn et al., "Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning" (2023)

Context engineering is the deliberate design of the information boundary presented to a model at each loop iteration. It treats context as an engineered runtime resource: assemble the right instructions, state, evidence, tool results, memory, constraints, and task history for the next decision instead of treating the context window as a passive transcript.

Why it matters

In long-running agents, the model is only as good as the slice of the world it can see. Context engineering turns prompt assembly into a measurable system problem involving relevance, freshness, ordering, provenance, budget, and failure recovery.

Core engineering concepts

  • Context as a runtime resource with hard token and soft attention budgets
  • System instructions, task state, working state, evidence, tool results, and user constraints as distinct context classes
  • Freshness, relevance, authority, and provenance scoring for candidate context
  • Context assembly policies that differ by task phase and loop state
  • Priority ordering and conflict resolution between instructions and evidence
  • Context budget allocation across instructions, history, retrieval, tools, and output reserve
  • Context window saturation and degradation under long trajectories
  • Sensitive-context minimization and least-privilege context exposure
  • Observability of context composition, dropped items, truncation, and failures
  • Evaluation of context quality separately from model quality

Real-world build

Build an agent that receives the same task over ten iterations but dynamically changes its context composition based on the current state, retrieved evidence, unresolved errors, and remaining token budget. Log exactly what entered and left the context on every iteration.

Common failure mode

Treating context as “the conversation so far” and blindly appending every new observation. The result is larger prompts, poorer signal-to-noise ratio, stale instructions, and hidden budget failures.

Further reading

  • OpenAI — Context engineering guidance and agent-building documentation
  • Anthropic — context and long-context engineering guidance
  • Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts” (2023)

Context architecture defines the layers and ownership rules for assembling model-visible state. A robust system separates relatively stable instructions from volatile task state, retrieved knowledge, ephemeral tool outputs, memory, policies, and loop diagnostics so each component can be refreshed independently.

Why it matters

Without architectural boundaries, every iteration becomes a giant prompt-construction function. Separating context layers makes agents easier to cache, test, secure, debug, and evolve.

Core engineering concepts

  • Static versus dynamic context layers
  • Identity, policy, task, state, evidence, memory, tool-output, and scratchpad partitions
  • Context ownership and write permissions by subsystem
  • Instruction precedence and conflict resolution
  • Canonical state versus derived context
  • Context templates versus runtime-generated sections
  • Per-agent, per-task, per-step, and shared context scopes
  • Context interfaces and schemas between orchestrator components
  • Cacheable context segments and invalidation boundaries
  • Context versioning for reproducibility and regression analysis

Real-world build

Design a context builder with typed sections and explicit ownership: a policy layer, task specification, current state snapshot, evidence set, tool results, and memory summary. Make each layer independently replaceable and trace the final assembled context.

Common failure mode

Mixing authoritative state with model-generated summaries so thoroughly that the system can no longer tell what is ground truth, what is derived, and what is stale.

Further reading

  • Agent runtime documentation on state/context separation
  • Research on structured prompting and context management
  • Model Context Protocol specification — standardized context/tool interfaces

Dynamic context selection chooses which candidate information should be exposed for the current model action rather than sending every available artifact. Selection can use task relevance, recency, confidence, source authority, loop state, dependency relationships, and expected utility.

Why it matters

The frontier problem is no longer “can the model fit everything?” but “which information deserves scarce attention right now?” Good selection improves reliability while reducing latency and cost.

Core engineering concepts

  • Relevance scoring versus exact-match filtering
  • Recency and temporal validity
  • Source authority and evidence trust levels
  • Confidence-aware context inclusion
  • Diversity and redundancy control
  • Dependency-aware retrieval for related artifacts
  • Query expansion and contextual query rewriting
  • Reranking and top-k selection policies
  • Adaptive context selection driven by intermediate failures
  • Failure-aware fallback from compact context to broader retrieval

Real-world build

Implement a selector that starts with a compact evidence bundle and expands retrieval only when an evaluator identifies a missing fact, dependency, or unresolved uncertainty.

Common failure mode

Choosing context solely by vector similarity and assuming the nearest chunks are automatically the most useful evidence for the next action.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-augmented generation literature
  • Research on selective context and long-context utilization
  • Agent evaluation literature on retrieval/context failures

Context compaction converts a growing trajectory into a smaller representation while preserving the information needed for future decisions. Unlike naive summarization, engineering-grade compaction must preserve unresolved tasks, decisions, constraints, evidence, failures, provenance, and actionable state.

Why it matters

Long-horizon agents eventually hit token, latency, or attention limits. Compaction is therefore a control mechanism for keeping the loop alive rather than an optional prompt optimization.

Core engineering concepts

  • Lossy versus lossless context reduction
  • Summarization checkpoints and rolling state summaries
  • Preservation of open tasks, decisions, constraints, and blockers
  • Fact versus inference separation during compression
  • Provenance retention and source linking
  • Importance scoring before deletion
  • Compaction triggers based on token, step, cost, or state thresholds
  • Hierarchical summaries from raw events to episode summaries
  • Compaction quality evaluation and information-loss testing
  • Selective re-expansion when the compacted representation is insufficient

Real-world build

Build a trajectory compressor that emits a structured state summary after a fixed number of steps, then verify on held-out tasks that the compressed agent can still recover required facts and continue execution.

Common failure mode

Summarizing everything into prose with no explicit state schema. Important constraints disappear, temporal order collapses, and the next iteration confidently reasons from a distorted memory.

Further reading

  • Long-context utilization research
  • Context compression and summarization research
  • Agent runtime documentation on compaction/checkpoint strategies

Context caching reduces repeated work by reusing stable prompt segments, retrieval results, tool catalogs, or other context components when their validity window allows it. The engineering problem is deciding what is safe to cache, for how long, and when invalidation is mandatory.

Why it matters

Repeated context construction can dominate an agent’s cost and latency even when the model itself is fast. Caching turns stable context into reusable infrastructure, but stale caches can quietly corrupt the loop.

Core engineering concepts

  • Stable versus volatile context segments
  • Prompt-prefix caching and cache locality
  • Retrieval-result caching
  • Tool-catalog and capability caching
  • Cache keys and context identity
  • TTLs and event-driven invalidation
  • Model-version-aware cache invalidation
  • User/tenant isolation for cached context
  • Cache hit-rate, token-saved, latency-saved, and correctness metrics
  • Fallback behavior when cache freshness cannot be established

Real-world build

Instrument an agent with a cached stable instruction layer and a shorter-lived evidence cache. Measure token savings and latency while deliberately introducing stale evidence to test invalidation behavior.

Common failure mode

Caching everything without tracking provenance or freshness, producing fast but incorrect decisions that are difficult to diagnose because the stale artifact looks legitimate.

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol 2026-07-28 specification — cacheable list results
  • Provider documentation for prompt/context caching
  • Distributed-systems literature on cache invalidation

Context provenance records where every important piece of model-visible information came from, when it was retrieved, how trustworthy it is, and which subsystem introduced it. Context security applies the same discipline to permission boundaries, untrusted content, and injection-resistant assembly.

Why it matters

An agent cannot reliably evaluate evidence it cannot provenance. Provenance is also a security control: it helps distinguish trusted policy from untrusted web pages, tool output, memory entries, and user-supplied instructions.

Core engineering concepts

  • Origin metadata for retrieved and generated context
  • Trust tiers for system policy, application state, tools, memory, and external content
  • Provenance identifiers and source timestamps
  • Instruction/data separation
  • Indirect prompt injection from retrieved content and tools
  • Untrusted-context sanitization and boundary marking
  • Least-privilege context exposure
  • Sensitive data minimization and redaction
  • Provenance-aware auditing and forensic reconstruction
  • Evaluation of context poisoning and malicious-context scenarios

Real-world build

Construct a research agent where every evidence item carries source, timestamp, trust class, and retrieval path. Prevent external documents from silently overriding higher-priority system policy and record all provenance decisions.

Common failure mode

Treating retrieved text as trusted instructions. A malicious document, memory item, or tool output can then redirect the loop even though the primary system prompt is secure.

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol security and authorization documentation
  • OWASP guidance on prompt injection and agentic application security
  • Research on indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning

Context state management makes the information required to continue a loop explicit, durable, and reconstructible. Snapshots and checkpoints separate recoverable agent state from transient model context so long-running work can pause, resume, branch, and replay without reconstructing the entire history from scratch.

Why it matters

Long-running agents fail for reasons that have nothing to do with model quality: process crashes, timeouts, tool failures, deployments, human approvals, or context exhaustion. Durable snapshots turn those failures into recoverable state transitions.

Core engineering concepts

  • Canonical state versus rendered context
  • Checkpoint boundaries and snapshot frequency
  • Deterministic reconstruction of model-visible context
  • State serialization and schema evolution
  • Resumability after tool, network, or process failure
  • Branching and replay from prior checkpoints
  • Idempotent state restoration
  • Versioning state alongside prompts and tools
  • Partial progress and subtask checkpointing
  • Consistency between durable state and external side effects

Real-world build

Build a research agent that checkpoints after every major subtask. Kill the process mid-run, restart it from the latest checkpoint, and prove that it resumes without repeating already-committed external actions.

Common failure mode

Treating the conversation transcript as the system of record. A transcript is neither a reliable workflow state machine nor a safe recovery mechanism when external side effects have already occurred.

Further reading

  • Durable execution patterns in modern agent runtimes
  • Distributed-systems literature on checkpoints and recovery
  • Workflow-engine documentation on resumable execution

Reversible compaction reduces context volume while preserving enough structure to selectively reconstruct detail later. The goal is not merely to summarize, but to retain anchors, provenance, unresolved questions, and references that allow the system to recover detail when a later loop step needs it.

Why it matters

Irreversible summarization can quietly erase the exact evidence needed to solve a future problem. A production loop therefore needs a controlled boundary between compressed working context and reconstructable source material.

Core engineering concepts

  • Hierarchical summaries and abstraction levels
  • Lossy versus loss-minimizing compaction
  • Preserving source anchors and provenance
  • Open-issue and unresolved-decision retention
  • Selective re-expansion and targeted rereads
  • Compression triggers based on context pressure
  • Compaction quality evaluation
  • Reconstruction latency and retrieval cost
  • Compaction/version lineage
  • Detecting when compressed state is insufficient

Real-world build

Build a coding agent that compacts a large repository investigation into a structured working brief, then selectively re-expands exact files and prior evidence when a regression is detected.

Common failure mode

Summarizing everything into one prose blob and deleting the source references. The agent becomes unable to distinguish remembered conclusions from the evidence that produced them.

Further reading

  • Long-context management research
  • Retrieval and source-grounding literature
  • Agent runtime documentation on context compaction

Context caching reuses stable portions of model-visible state or computation across loop iterations rather than rebuilding and retransmitting identical material. The engineering problem is to identify reusable context safely while respecting freshness, invalidation, privacy, and model/provider semantics.

Why it matters

Agent loops repeatedly resend stable instructions, schemas, policies, and reference material. Caching can reduce latency and cost, but stale cached context can produce systematic errors that are harder to notice than ordinary prompt mistakes.

Core engineering concepts

  • Static-prefix versus dynamic-context partitioning
  • Prompt/prefix cache eligibility
  • Cache keys and canonicalization
  • Freshness windows and invalidation
  • Model/version-aware cache boundaries
  • Per-tenant and per-user cache isolation
  • Sensitive-context leakage risks
  • Cache hit-rate and cost observability
  • Cache warming and cold-start behavior
  • Consistency between cached and authoritative state

Real-world build

Build a multi-step agent with stable policy and tool-schema prefixes. Measure cache hit rate, latency, and spend, then introduce an intentional policy update and verify that invalidation propagates correctly.

Common failure mode

Caching content whose validity depends on changing user, permission, or system state. The loop appears fast and reliable while operating on stale assumptions.

Further reading

  • Provider documentation for prompt/prefix caching
  • Caching theory and distributed invalidation patterns
  • Agent performance engineering references

Context lineage records where each model-visible fact, instruction, decision, and tool result came from, while conflict resolution determines which competing pieces of context should control behavior. This makes context auditable instead of opaque.

Why it matters

Agents routinely combine system policy, user instructions, retrieved documents, memory, tool output, and model-generated summaries. Without explicit authority and lineage, stale or lower-trust information can overwrite authoritative state.

Core engineering concepts

  • Source provenance metadata
  • Authority ranking across context sources
  • Temporal validity and freshness
  • Contradiction detection
  • Conflict-resolution policies
  • Derived facts versus source facts
  • Evidence chains and citation propagation
  • User-visible versus internal provenance
  • Lineage capture in traces
  • Forensic reconstruction of a decision

Real-world build

Build a support agent that stores provenance for every retrieved fact and rejects a newer but lower-authority document when it conflicts with a verified policy source.

Common failure mode

Flattening every input into undifferentiated text and asking the model to “figure out” which source wins. That makes precedence implicit, untestable, and vulnerable to prompt injection.

Further reading

  • Data lineage and provenance systems
  • Knowledge provenance research
  • Policy-based data integration

Context security controls which information an agent is allowed to observe, retain, combine, and pass onward. It treats context exposure as a capability boundary rather than assuming that all available information should be visible to the model.

Why it matters

Even a correct tool policy can fail if sensitive data is placed into the model context without need. Context itself can leak secrets, cross tenant boundaries, or carry malicious instructions between trust domains.

Core engineering concepts

  • Least-privilege context exposure
  • Per-user, per-tenant, and per-agent context scopes
  • Secret and credential exclusion
  • Prompt-injection-resistant source isolation
  • Untrusted retrieval boundaries
  • Cross-tenant contamination prevention
  • Memory/context access policies
  • Redaction before model exposure
  • Context egress controls
  • Security auditing of context assembly

Real-world build

Build a multi-tenant agent that retrieves customer records while enforcing tenant-scoped context filters, secret redaction, and explicit policy checks before data reaches the model.

Common failure mode

Assuming that secure tools automatically imply secure context. Once sensitive or attacker-controlled content enters the context, the model can potentially propagate it into later actions.

Further reading

  • OWASP agentic security guidance
  • Least-privilege and information-flow security literature
  • Enterprise AI data-boundary patterns
Level 2

Prompt Loop Engineering

The foundations from Level 1 applied to the smallest, cheapest unit of loop engineering: a single prompt refining itself, or a short chain of prompts refining each other. This is where most practitioners start building real loops.

Topics: 19 Est. time: ~4.5 hrs Prerequisites: Level 0, Level 1

Extend the context-aware loop into an acting system that selects tools, validates arguments, checks authority, executes with idempotency and timeouts, normalizes results, and verifies postconditions.

Why this project exists

Modern agents are integration systems. The portfolio must demonstrate that you can make external actions reliable and bounded, not merely generate tool calls.

Builds on the previous level

Reuses L0 replay/evidence and L1 context contracts; every tool call becomes a first-class loop event.

Architecture flow: Goal + Context → Tool Router → Permission Gate → Tool Runtime → Postcondition Verifier → Reliability Evidence → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • tool contracts
  • JSON Schema validation
  • tool selection
  • idempotency keys
  • timeouts
  • retry budgets
  • circuit breakers
  • permission checks
  • result normalization
  • postconditions
  • integration testing
  • side-effect accounting

Recommended implementation stack

Python/TypeScript, FastAPI, Pydantic/JSON Schema, Docker, pytest, SQLite/Postgres

Build sequence

1 · Contract

Specify schemas, side effects, permissions, timeouts, expected results, and idempotency behavior.

2 · Route

Select tools and reject unsupported, ambiguous, or dangerous actions before execution.

3 · Execute

Add timeout, retry, idempotency key, circuit breaker, and structured error handling.

4 · Verify

Require explicit postconditions before success can be recorded.

5 · Stress

Inject malformed inputs, partial failures, stale results, duplicate execution, and dependency outages.

6 · Package

Publish tool contracts, sequence traces, reliability numbers, and a failure postmortem.

Definition of done

  • Unsafe calls are rejected before execution.
  • Retries cannot duplicate protected side effects.
  • Every successful action has a verifier signal.
  • Reliability is measured per tool and per workflow.
  • Failure handling is deterministic under replay.
  • At least three real or sandboxed integrations are demonstrated.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • tool contracts
  • sequence diagrams
  • failure injection tests
  • reliability dashboard
  • policy rules
  • integration tests
  • postmortem
  • demo

Public artifact

`reliable-agent-tools`: three-integration agent with deterministic failure handling and contract tests.

Project-specific failure to avoid

A demo that calls APIs successfully but cannot prove what happens on timeout, duplication, denial, or partial failure.

Market research basis · 2026

Paragon’s 2026 research highlights integration reliability as a major blocker; Docker reports security and tool-readiness as major enterprise scaling challenges.

Portfolio handoff

L3 wraps these tool capabilities in MCP and connects agents through A2A.

Prompt iteration is the simplest possible loop: send a prompt, inspect the response, adjust the prompt, and send it again. It applies Level 1's "iteration" concept at the smallest possible scale — a single message exchange.

Why it matters

Every more advanced pattern in this level — chaining, recursion, tree search — is prompt iteration composed with itself. Getting this base case right (what actually changes between attempts) makes everything built on top of it easier.

Core concepts

  • What changes between iterations: instruction, examples, or constraints
  • Manual iteration vs. automated iteration
  • Convergence signals for a single-prompt loop

Real-world example

Tightening a summarization prompt across three passes by adding an explicit word-count constraint after the first output ran long.

Common mistake

Changing multiple variables at once between iterations (tone, length, and structure together), which makes it impossible to tell which change actually caused an improvement.

Further reading

  • Anthropic's prompt engineering documentation on iterative refinement

A reflection prompt explicitly asks a model to critique its own prior output before producing a revised version — "Review your answer above for factual errors, then rewrite it." It's the prompt-level implementation of Level 1's reflection concept.

Why it matters

A well-worded reflection prompt can catch a meaningful share of surface-level errors (formatting, missed constraints) cheaply, without any extra tooling.

Core concepts

  • Specific vs. generic reflection instructions
  • Reflection checklists vs. open-ended critique
  • The blind-spot limit (same as Level 1's Reflection topic)

Real-world example

"Check your draft against these five requirements one by one and flag any that are missing" outperforms a generic "check your work" prompt because it gives the reflection step a concrete checklist.

Common mistake

Using a vague reflection instruction ("double check this") that gives the model no concrete criteria to check against, producing a superficial pass that rarely changes anything.

Further reading

  • Madaan et al., "Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback" (2023)

Self-critique goes one step further than reflection: rather than just flagging issues, the model is prompted to produce a structured critique — separate from the revision — that can be logged, scored, or fed to a different evaluator before any rewrite happens.

Why it matters

Separating critique from revision lets you inspect and debug the "why" behind a change, and lets a different, potentially more capable model or process act on the critique instead of the original generator blindly revising itself.

Core concepts

  • Critique as a distinct output from revision
  • Structured critique formats (issue, severity, suggested fix)
  • Cross-model critique (a different model critiques the generator)

Real-world example

A writing pipeline where a "critic" pass outputs a JSON list of specific issues with severities, which a separate "editor" pass then addresses one at a time.

Common mistake

Letting the same call both critique and revise in one unstructured response, which makes it hard to verify the critique was actually acted on rather than just restated.

Further reading

  • Madaan et al., "Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback" (2023)

Prompt chaining breaks a task into a fixed sequence of separate prompts, where each prompt's output becomes the next prompt's input — outline, then draft, then edit, for example — rather than asking one prompt to do everything at once.

Why it matters

Splitting a task into focused steps generally produces more reliable results than one large, multi-instruction prompt, because each step has a narrower job and a checkable output.

Core concepts

  • Fixed linear chains vs. adaptive chains
  • Intermediate output validation between links
  • Chain length vs. error-accumulation trade-off

Real-world example

A report-writing chain: research prompt → outline prompt → section-drafting prompt (run per section) → final edit prompt, each with a narrow, checkable job.

Common mistake

Chaining too many steps without validating intermediate outputs, so an early error silently propagates and compounds through every later link in the chain.

Further reading

  • Wu et al., "AI Chains: Transparent and Controllable Human-AI Interaction by Chaining Large Language Model Prompts" (2022)

Recursive prompting applies the same prompt template to a problem's sub-parts, and to those sub-parts' sub-parts, until pieces are small enough to solve directly — then combines the results back up. It's divide-and-conquer, implemented in prompts.

Why it matters

Recursive prompting handles problems whose size isn't known in advance and that decompose naturally (nested documents, hierarchical codebases) far better than a fixed-length chain.

Core concepts

  • Base case and recursive case for prompts
  • Result aggregation across recursive calls
  • Recursion depth limits (loop budget applied recursively)

Real-world example

Summarizing a book by recursively summarizing each chapter, then summarizing the chapter summaries, until a single top-level summary remains.

Common mistake

Omitting a hard recursion-depth limit, which risks the same runaway-cost failure mode as any unbounded loop, just spread across a tree instead of a single chain.

Further reading

  • Literature on recursive summarization and map-reduce prompting patterns

Tree prompting explores multiple candidate continuations from the same point at once — a branching structure — evaluates each branch, and continues down the most promising ones. It's Level 1's "search" applied directly to prompt-driven reasoning.

Why it matters

A single linear chain commits early to one reasoning path; tree prompting hedges against an early wrong turn by keeping several paths alive until there's evidence for which is best.

Core concepts

  • Branching factor and tree depth
  • Per-branch evaluation and scoring
  • Pruning weak branches to control cost

Real-world example

Tree-of-Thoughts solving a puzzle by generating three different next moves, scoring each with a heuristic evaluator, and only continuing the top-scoring branch.

Common mistake

Growing the tree without a pruning strategy — cost grows combinatorially with depth and branching factor, quickly outweighing the marginal quality gain from extra branches.

Further reading

  • Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (2023)

Graph prompting generalizes tree prompting by allowing branches to merge back together, not just split — reasoning paths can share and combine intermediate results instead of staying strictly separate until one "wins."

Why it matters

Some problems benefit from combining partial insights from multiple reasoning paths (e.g., "path A found the right formula, path B found the right constraint") — a tree can't represent that merge, but a graph can.

Core concepts

  • Nodes as partial thoughts, edges as transformations
  • Aggregation (merge) operations across nodes
  • Cycles and how to prevent infinite re-merging

Real-world example

Graph-of-Thoughts combining a "generate constraints" branch and a "generate candidate solutions" branch into a single node that checks candidates against constraints.

Common mistake

Allowing unrestricted merges without a cycle-prevention rule, which can create loops within the reasoning graph itself, separate from the outer refinement loop.

Further reading

  • Besta et al., "Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models" (2023)

Prompt repair is the targeted act of fixing a specific defect in a prompt — an ambiguous instruction, a missing constraint, a misleading example — rather than rewriting the prompt from scratch each time something goes wrong.

Why it matters

Diagnosing exactly which part of a prompt caused a failure (an example, an instruction, formatting guidance) lets you fix that one part with confidence instead of guessing at a full rewrite.

Core concepts

  • Isolating the specific failing prompt component
  • Minimal-diff repair vs. full rewrite
  • Regression risk when repairing shared prompt templates

Real-world example

Noticing outputs consistently ignore a length constraint, and fixing only that one instruction's phrasing rather than rewriting the entire system prompt.

Common mistake

Rewriting an entire prompt template to fix one failure mode, which risks silently breaking other behaviors that the original wording was handling correctly.

Further reading

  • Prompt-versioning and regression-testing practices from prompt IDE documentation

Prompt optimization applies Level 1's optimization concept systematically: define a measurable objective, generate prompt variants, score each against a held-out set of test cases, and keep the best — either manually or via an automated search process.

Why it matters

It replaces "I feel like this prompt is better" with a measured comparison, which matters enormously once a prompt is running at scale in production.

Core concepts

  • Held-out test sets for prompt evaluation
  • Automated prompt search (e.g., variant generation and scoring)
  • Overfitting a prompt to its test set

Real-world example

Running five prompt variants against 50 held-out support tickets, scoring each variant's resolution accuracy, and promoting the highest scorer to production.

Common mistake

Optimizing against a small or unrepresentative test set, which produces a prompt that scores well in evaluation but underperforms on the true distribution of real inputs.

Further reading

  • Pryzant et al., "Automatic Prompt Optimization with 'Gradient Descent' and Beam Search" (2023)

Loop termination is the explicit rule that decides when to stop iterating: a quality threshold met, an attempt-count budget exhausted, no improvement across the last N passes, or an external timeout. Every prompt loop needs one, even a simple one.

Why it matters

Without a termination rule, a loop either stops arbitrarily (wasting quality left on the table) or never stops (wasting cost indefinitely) — it's the single most commonly missing piece in prompt loop implementations.

Core concepts

  • Threshold-based termination
  • Budget-based termination (max attempts, max cost, max time)
  • Plateau detection (stop when improvement stalls)

Real-world example

A refinement loop that stops when either the evaluator score exceeds 0.9, or five attempts have passed, or the last two scores differ by less than 0.02 (a plateau).

Common mistake

Using only a fixed attempt count with no quality threshold, which wastes compute on easy cases that converged early and still under-delivers on hard cases that needed more attempts.

Further reading

  • Convergence-criteria literature from classical optimization (see Level 1 — Optimization)

Failure handling is what a loop does when termination is reached without success — the budget ran out and the quality bar still wasn't met. Options include falling back to the best-so-far attempt, escalating to a human, or failing loudly with a clear error.

Why it matters

A loop that silently returns its worst attempt after exhausting its budget is far more dangerous than one that fails visibly — silent degraded output erodes trust in the whole system.

Core concepts

  • Best-so-far fallback
  • Human escalation on exhausted budget
  • Explicit failure signaling vs. silent degradation

Real-world example

A support-reply loop that, after exhausting its retries without reaching a confidence threshold, routes the ticket to a human agent instead of sending its best (but unverified) guess.

Common mistake

Treating "loop finished" as synonymous with "loop succeeded," when a loop can finish by exhausting its budget without ever meeting the quality bar.

Further reading

  • Site-reliability-engineering literature on graceful degradation and fallback design

Context recycling is deliberately reusing parts of a prior iteration's context (a system prompt, a retrieved document, an earlier critique) in the next iteration, instead of rebuilding everything from scratch each pass.

Why it matters

Rebuilding full context every iteration is expensive and can lose valuable earlier information; recycling the right pieces keeps cost down while preserving continuity across attempts.

Core concepts

  • What to recycle vs. regenerate each pass
  • Stale-context risk (recycled info that's since become wrong)
  • Caching recycled segments for cost efficiency

Real-world example

Reusing a retrieved reference document across all three revision passes of an essay, instead of re-running retrieval every single iteration.

Common mistake

Recycling a piece of context that's no longer accurate for the current iteration (e.g., an outdated plan), which silently misleads later reasoning steps.

Further reading

  • Prompt-caching documentation from major LLM API providers

Compression reduces prior context — history, retrieved documents, past critiques — down to its essential content before feeding it into the next iteration, typically via summarization or structured extraction.

Why it matters

Compression is how long-running loops stay within context limits and keep the model's attention on what matters, rather than diluting it across an ever-growing transcript.

Core concepts

  • Summarization vs. structured extraction
  • Lossy compression risk (dropping something that mattered)
  • Progressive compression across many iterations

Real-world example

A research loop that compresses each new source into three bullet points of relevant findings, rather than carrying the full source text forward every iteration.

Common mistake

Over-compressing and losing a specific detail (an exact number, a caveat) that turns out to matter several iterations later, when it's too late to recover.

Further reading

  • Literature on recursive/hierarchical summarization (see also Level 2 — Recursive Prompting)

Expansion is compression's counterpart: deliberately adding detail, examples, or context back in when a compressed representation turns out to be insufficient for the current iteration's needs.

Why it matters

A loop that only ever compresses eventually loses too much detail to make good decisions; knowing when and what to expand back in keeps a long loop from degrading over time.

Core concepts

  • Detecting when compressed context is insufficient
  • Selective re-expansion (only the relevant part)
  • Expansion vs. re-retrieval trade-off

Real-world example

A coding agent that re-reads the full source of a file (rather than its earlier summary) once a bug is suspected to be in that specific file.

Common mistake

Re-expanding everything back to its raw form "just in case," which undoes the benefit compression was providing and reintroduces the original context-bloat problem.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) literature on selective re-retrieval

Hierarchical prompts organize instructions in layers of increasing specificity — a stable system-level prompt, a task-level prompt beneath it, and a per-iteration prompt on top — so that only the most volatile layer needs to change between iterations.

Why it matters

Separating stable instructions from per-iteration specifics keeps loops maintainable: fixing a bug in the "always true" rules doesn't require touching every iteration's dynamic content.

Core concepts

  • System / task / iteration layering
  • Inheritance and override between layers
  • Caching stable upper layers for cost efficiency

Real-world example

A code-review loop with a fixed system prompt ("you are a strict reviewer"), a stable task prompt ("review this PR for security issues"), and a per-iteration prompt containing just the current diff.

Common mistake

Flattening everything into one undifferentiated prompt block, which makes it hard to update shared rules without risking unintended changes to iteration-specific behavior.

Further reading

  • Prompt-templating and layering practices from prompt-management platforms

A meta prompt is a prompt whose job is to generate or improve another prompt — turning prompt engineering itself into a loop-driven, model-assisted process rather than a purely manual one.

Why it matters

Meta prompts let a model help scale prompt iteration across many tasks or many variants at once, which becomes essential once you're maintaining more prompts than you can hand-tune individually.

Core concepts

  • Prompts that generate prompts
  • Meta-prompt evaluation (how do you judge a generated prompt?)
  • Risk of the meta-loop inheriting the base loop's blind spots

Real-world example

Asking a model to draft three variations of a classification prompt targeting a specific failure mode observed in production logs, then testing all three.

Common mistake

Trusting a meta-generated prompt without testing it the same way a human-written one would be tested — a generated prompt still needs the full evaluation and optimization treatment.

Further reading

  • Zhou et al., "Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers" (2022)

Prompt debugging is the systematic process of finding why a prompt produces an unwanted output — isolating variables, testing components in isolation, and reproducing failures reliably — borrowed directly from software debugging practice.

Why it matters

Prompts fail for specific, findable reasons (an ambiguous instruction, a misleading example, conflicting constraints); treating failures as mysterious wastes far more time than debugging them systematically.

Core concepts

  • Reproducing a failure reliably before trying to fix it
  • Bisecting a prompt to isolate the failing component
  • Distinguishing prompt bugs from model limitations

Real-world example

Removing a few-shot example one at a time to find which specific example was causing the model to copy an unwanted formatting pattern.

Common mistake

Changing several parts of a prompt at once while debugging, which — as with prompt iteration generally — makes it impossible to attribute the fix to any specific change.

Further reading

  • General software-debugging methodology (bisection, minimal reproduction) applied to prompts

Prompt benchmarking is running a fixed, representative test set against a prompt (or several candidate prompts) and recording quantitative results, so quality changes over time — or across model versions — are measurable rather than anecdotal.

Why it matters

Without a benchmark, you can't tell whether a "small tweak" to a production prompt actually helped, hurt, or did nothing — and you can't catch silent regressions when the underlying model changes.

Core concepts

  • Representative, fixed test sets
  • Regression testing across prompt or model versions
  • Benchmark drift (a benchmark becoming outdated or gamed)

Real-world example

Re-running a fixed 100-case benchmark every time a model version updates, to catch cases where a prompt that worked on the old model silently underperforms on the new one.

Common mistake

Reusing the same benchmark set indefinitely without auditing it, allowing prompts to become implicitly over-tuned to that specific set rather than the real task distribution.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Evaluation Loops for benchmark design in depth
Level 3

Agent Loop Engineering

Agent architectures now meet the interoperability layer: named loop patterns, specialized agent roles, MCP tool connectivity, A2A agent communication, capability contracts, discovery, authorization, and the boundaries required for independently deployed agent systems.

Topics: 39 Est. time: ~10 hrs Prerequisites: Level 0–2

Turn L2 into a multi-agent system: expose capabilities through MCP, advertise agent capabilities, delegate work through A2A, authenticate every boundary, return structured artifacts, and trace the complete handoff.

Why this project exists

The market is moving toward interoperable agent ecosystems. The project proves protocol literacy plus the engineering discipline required when control crosses process and vendor boundaries.

Builds on the previous level

Reuses L2 tool contracts and permission gates; MCP exposes those capabilities while A2A carries delegated work between agents.

Architecture flow: Client Agent → Capability Registry → MCP Boundary → A2A Handoff → Specialist Agent → Trace + Artifacts → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • MCP architecture
  • A2A task lifecycle
  • capability discovery
  • Agent Cards
  • task handoff
  • authentication
  • authorization
  • artifact exchange
  • protocol versioning
  • timeout propagation
  • cross-agent tracing
  • failure recovery

Recommended implementation stack

Python/TypeScript, MCP SDK, A2A SDK, FastAPI, Docker Compose, OpenTelemetry

Build sequence

1 · Expose

Wrap L2 tools as typed MCP resources/tools with explicit permissions and result contracts.

2 · Advertise

Create capability metadata and Agent Cards with supported tasks, auth, versions, and constraints.

3 · Delegate

Implement A2A task submission, status updates, artifact return, cancellation, and timeout behavior.

4 · Secure

Bind identity and authorization to every handoff; prevent confused-deputy behavior.

5 · Test

Run cross-agent failures: unavailable agent, wrong capability, stale artifact, auth denial, duplicate task.

6 · Package

Publish protocol traces, interoperability matrix, Agent Cards, and a recorded end-to-end handoff.

Definition of done

  • MCP tools are discoverable and contract-tested.
  • A2A delegation has explicit lifecycle states.
  • Every handoff carries identity and authorization context.
  • Artifacts are typed and traceable to their producing agent.
  • Protocol failures are recoverable or escalated.
  • The complete network can be replayed from traces.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • Agent Cards
  • MCP schemas
  • A2A traces
  • auth tests
  • interoperability matrix
  • artifact lineage
  • failure postmortem
  • demo

Public artifact

`agent-network-lab`: MCP tool server + A2A specialist network with traceable task handoffs.

Project-specific failure to avoid

Two agents calling each other through ad-hoc HTTP without capability contracts, identity, or lifecycle semantics.

Market research basis · 2026

A2A and MCP are complementary standards: MCP handles agent-to-tool/resource access while A2A handles agent-to-agent discovery and delegation. Current 2026 ecosystem work continues to formalize this separation.

Portfolio handoff

L4 persists the network’s state, tasks, artifacts, and memory across restarts.

ReAct (Reason + Act) interleaves explicit reasoning steps with tool-use actions in a single loop: the model reasons about what it needs, takes an action (like a search or a calculation), observes the result, and reasons again — repeating until it has enough to answer.

Why it matters

ReAct is the base pattern behind most modern tool-using agents, including Claude's own tool-use loop: reasoning alone can be wrong about the world, and acting alone has no way to plan — interleaving both compounds their strengths.

Core concepts

  • Thought → Action → Observation cycle
  • Grounding reasoning in real tool outputs, not assumptions
  • When to stop acting and commit to a final answer

Real-world example

An agent answering "what's the weather-adjusted attendance forecast for this outdoor event" by reasoning about what data it needs, calling a weather tool, reasoning about the result, then calling a calculation tool.

Common mistake

Letting the model act without an explicit reasoning step first, which tends to produce plausible-looking but poorly targeted tool calls.

Further reading

  • Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models" (2022)

Reflexion is the full agent framework built around Level 1's reflection concept: after a failed attempt at a task, the agent writes a natural-language "reflection" describing what went wrong, stores it in an episodic memory buffer, and carries it into the next attempt — verbal reinforcement instead of weight updates.

Why it matters
