It shows how far pure prompting can substitute for fine-tuning on some tasks: the agent's "learning" is entirely in accumulated natural-language notes, not gradient updates.

Core concepts

  • Verbal reinforcement (learning via written self-notes)
  • Episodic memory buffer across attempts
  • Same blind-spot limitation as any self-critique loop

Real-world example

A coding-puzzle agent that fails a test, writes "I misunderstood the edge case where the list is empty," and uses that note to avoid the same mistake on the next attempt.

Common mistake

Relying on Reflexion alone for tasks with objectively checkable answers, where a cheap external verifier would catch errors the model's own reflection consistently misses.

Further reading

  • Shinn et al., "Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning" (2023)

Tree of Thoughts (ToT) is the full framework built on Level 2's tree prompting concept: it formalizes a self-evaluation step at each node and a search strategy (breadth-first or depth-first-with-backtracking) for deciding which branches to expand.

Why it matters

ToT was the framework that demonstrated deliberate, search-based problem solving substantially outperforms single-chain-of-thought prompting on tasks with multiple plausible next steps.

Core concepts

  • Thought generation, state evaluation, search algorithm (the three ToT components)
  • Backtracking on dead-end branches
  • Cost vs. quality trade-off relative to a single chain

Real-world example

Solving the "Game of 24" puzzle by generating several candidate next operations, scoring how promising each is, and backtracking away from branches that hit a dead end.

Common mistake

Applying ToT to tasks that only have one reasonable next step at each point — the extra search cost buys nothing when there's no real branching decision to make.

Further reading

  • Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (2023)

Graph of Thoughts (GoT) is the full framework built on Level 2's graph prompting concept, formalizing thoughts as graph vertices and transformations (generate, aggregate, refine, score) as operations on that graph — enabling merges that a tree structure can't represent.

Why it matters

GoT's aggregation operation lets an agent combine the best parts of multiple partial solutions into one — something ReAct's linear chain and ToT's strict tree both structurally cannot do.

Core concepts

  • Thoughts as graph vertices, operations as edges
  • Aggregation (merging multiple thoughts into one)
  • Volume — how much information a thought synthesizes

Real-world example

Merging a "candidate sort algorithm" thought and a "edge-case analysis" thought into one node that's both efficient and handles edge cases correctly.

Common mistake

Reaching for GoT's added complexity when a simpler tree or chain would do — the aggregation machinery only pays off when a task genuinely benefits from merging separate lines of reasoning.

Further reading

  • Besta et al., "Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models" (2023)

Plan-and-Execute separates an agent loop into two distinct phases: a planner produces a multi-step plan upfront, then an executor works through the plan step by step, calling the planner again only if a step fails or new information changes the plan's assumptions.

Why it matters

Compared to ReAct's interleaved reason-act-observe on every single step, Plan-and-Execute uses the (often more capable, more expensive) planning call sparingly — cheaper and more structured for tasks with a fairly predictable shape.

Core concepts

  • Upfront multi-step plan generation
  • Step-by-step execution against the plan
  • Re-planning triggers (step failure, new information)

Real-world example

A data-pipeline agent that plans "extract → transform → load → validate" once, then executes each stage, only re-invoking the planner if the "validate" stage reveals a schema mismatch.

Common mistake

Using Plan-and-Execute for highly unpredictable environments where nearly every step surfaces new information — the upfront plan becomes stale almost immediately, and ReAct's tighter loop fits better.

Further reading

  • LangChain and LangGraph documentation on the Plan-and-Execute agent pattern

Self-Discover has a model select and compose its own reasoning structure from a set of atomic reasoning modules (e.g., "break down the problem," "use analogies," "think step by step") before solving a task — discovering an approach rather than using a fixed, hand-designed prompt template.

Why it matters

It's a meta-prompting technique (Level 2) applied at the level of reasoning strategy: instead of a human pre-choosing chain-of-thought vs. tree-of-thoughts, the model picks the structure suited to the specific problem.

Core concepts

  • Atomic reasoning modules as building blocks
  • Task-adaptive structure selection
  • Composed reasoning structure as an intermediate, reusable artifact

Real-world example

A model facing a logic puzzle selecting "decompose into sub-problems" plus "verify each sub-solution," while facing a creative-writing task instead selecting "brainstorm alternatives" plus "critique for originality."

Common mistake

Skipping validation of the discovered structure itself — a poorly composed reasoning structure can be worse than a simple, well-tested default like plain chain-of-thought.

Further reading

  • Zhou et al., "Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures" (2024)

AutoGPT popularized the fully autonomous agent loop concept: a single agent given a high-level goal that repeatedly plans its own next sub-goal, executes it with available tools, and updates its own task list — running with minimal human intervention between steps.

Why it matters

It demonstrated both the appeal and the risk of high autonomy: impressive open-ended task pursuit, but also a clear case study in how ungated loops can spiral into unproductive or costly behavior without strong termination and evaluation design (Levels 1–2).

Core concepts

  • Self-generated sub-goals from a single high-level goal
  • Autonomous tool selection and execution
  • Minimal human-in-the-loop gating (and its risks)

Real-world example

Giving an AutoGPT-style agent the goal "research and summarize competitor pricing" and letting it decide on its own which searches to run and when it considers the task done.

Common mistake

Deploying this level of autonomy without a hard budget and human checkpoint — early AutoGPT-style agents were notorious for looping on unproductive sub-goals indefinitely.

Further reading

  • The AutoGPT open-source project documentation and post-mortems on early autonomous-agent failure modes

BabyAGI structures autonomous task pursuit around three explicit components run in a loop: a task-creation agent (adds new tasks based on results), a prioritization agent (reorders the task list), and an execution agent (does the top task) — making the otherwise implicit AutoGPT loop explicit and inspectable.

Why it matters

Splitting "decide what to do next" into separate creation and prioritization steps makes the loop's decision process legible — you can log and debug why a given task got inserted or reordered, unlike a single opaque planning call.

Core concepts

  • Explicit task list as persistent loop state
  • Separate creation, prioritization, and execution roles
  • Result-driven task-list growth

Real-world example

After executing "research topic X," the task-creation agent adds "summarize findings" and "identify open questions" as new tasks, which the prioritization agent then reorders against the existing list.

Common mistake

Letting the task-creation agent add tasks without any bound, producing an ever-growing list that the prioritization step can't meaningfully triage — a task-list version of unbounded context growth (Level 2 — Context).

Further reading

  • The BabyAGI open-source project documentation

CAMEL (Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Models) pairs two agents in fixed complementary roles — typically an "AI User" that issues instructions and an "AI Assistant" that carries them out — and lets them converse autonomously toward a shared task, with minimal human steering after the initial setup.

Why it matters

CAMEL was an early demonstration that role-play framing alone — no special tooling — can produce structured, on-task multi-turn collaboration between two instances of the same underlying model.

Core concepts

  • Role-play prompting as a coordination mechanism
  • Inception prompting (setting up roles and task at the start)
  • Conversational termination conditions between two agents

Real-world example

A "User" agent role-playing a product manager describing requirements, and an "Assistant" agent role-playing an engineer proposing an implementation, iterating until the User agent says the requirements are met.

Common mistake

Omitting a clear termination condition for the two-agent conversation, which can drift into circular exchanges that never converge on a concrete deliverable.

Further reading

  • Li et al., "CAMEL: Communicative Agents for 'Mind' Exploration of Large Language Model Society" (2023)

MetaGPT assigns agents distinct roles modeled on a real software company — product manager, architect, engineer, QA — and encodes standard operating procedures between them, so each role produces a specific structured artifact (a spec, a design doc, code, tests) that the next role consumes.

Why it matters

It shows how borrowing proven human organizational structure — clear roles, defined handoffs, structured intermediate artifacts — reduces the coordination failures that looser multi-agent conversations (like CAMEL's) are prone to.

Core concepts

  • Role specialization modeled on real organizations
  • Standardized operating procedures (SOPs) between roles
  • Structured artifacts as the interface between agents

Real-world example

A product-manager agent producing a structured requirements document that an architect agent consumes to produce a system design, which an engineer agent then implements.

Common mistake

Copying the role structure without the structured artifacts between them — the SOPs and defined document formats are what make the handoffs reliable, not the role labels alone.

Further reading

  • Hong et al., "MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework" (2023)

CrewAI structures a multi-agent system around a "crew" of agents, each with a defined role, goal, and backstory, working through a task list under either a sequential process (fixed order) or a hierarchical process (a manager agent delegates and reviews).

Why it matters

It packages the role-based coordination pattern (seen in MetaGPT) into a reusable framework with configurable process types, making it a common practical entry point for building production multi-agent crews.

Core concepts

  • Role, goal, and backstory as agent configuration
  • Sequential vs. hierarchical process types
  • Task assignment and delegation between crew members

Real-world example

A content-production crew with a "researcher" agent, a "writer" agent, and an "editor" agent running sequentially, each consuming the previous agent's output.

Common mistake

Using a hierarchical process with a manager agent for simple, predictable pipelines where a cheaper sequential process would produce the same result with less overhead.

Further reading

  • CrewAI project documentation on process types and role configuration

AutoGen models multi-agent systems as configurable "conversable agents" that exchange messages under flexible conversation patterns — two-agent chat, group chat with a selector deciding who speaks next, or nested conversations where one agent's turn is itself a sub-conversation.

Why it matters

Its group-chat pattern with a dynamic speaker-selection mechanism generalizes beyond fixed role pipelines (like MetaGPT or CrewAI's sequential mode) to open-ended discussions where who should speak next isn't known in advance.

Core concepts

  • Conversable agents as the base abstraction
  • Group chat with dynamic speaker selection
  • Nested conversations (a turn that's itself a sub-loop)

Real-world example

A group chat of a coder agent, a code-reviewer agent, and a user-proxy agent, where a selector picks the next speaker based on the current state of the conversation rather than a fixed turn order.

Common mistake

Using open-ended group chat for tasks with a genuinely fixed, predictable sequence — the dynamic selection overhead adds cost and unpredictability where a simple sequential chain would be both cheaper and more reliable.

Further reading

  • Wu et al., "AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation" (2023)

OpenAI's agent-building concepts center on "handoffs" — explicit transfer of a conversation from one specialized agent to another based on the request's nature — plus "guardrails," input/output checks that run alongside an agent to catch unsafe or off-scope behavior before it reaches the user.

Why it matters

Handoffs formalize a common production pattern — routing a request to the right specialized agent — as a first-class primitive rather than an ad-hoc routing prompt, and guardrails formalize safety checks as a parallel process rather than something baked only into the main prompt.

Core concepts

  • Handoffs (explicit agent-to-agent transfer)
  • Guardrails as parallel input/output validation
  • Tracing for debugging multi-agent execution

Real-world example

A general customer-service agent handing off to a specialized billing agent once it detects the request is billing-related, with a guardrail separately checking the billing agent never discloses another customer's data.

Common mistake

Treating guardrails as optional polish added at the end, rather than a parallel process designed alongside the agent from the start — retrofitting them is far harder than building them in from day one.

Further reading

  • OpenAI's documentation on agent handoffs, guardrails, and tracing

Swarm architectures favor many lightweight, narrowly-scoped agents coordinating through simple local rules and handoffs, rather than one heavyweight agent or a small number of complex, deeply-specified roles — trading individual agent sophistication for system-level flexibility and easier debugging per agent.

Why it matters

Small, single-purpose agents are individually easier to evaluate, test, and reason about than one large agent doing everything — swarm designs push complexity into the coordination layer instead of any single agent's prompt.

Core concepts

  • Many narrow agents vs. few broad agents
  • Local coordination rules instead of central control
  • Emergent system behavior from simple agent-level rules

Real-world example

A customer-support swarm where a routing agent hands off to one of a dozen single-topic agents (billing, shipping, returns), each with a small, easy-to-audit prompt.

Common mistake

Over-fragmenting a task into too many narrow agents, which can push the real complexity into an increasingly fragile handoff/routing layer instead of actually simplifying the system.

Further reading

  • OpenAI's Swarm experimental framework documentation on lightweight multi-agent coordination

Task decomposition is the specific skill of breaking a high-level goal into sub-tasks that are small enough for individual agents to execute reliably, with clear boundaries for what each sub-task needs as input and produces as output.

Why it matters

Every multi-agent framework in this level depends on good decomposition — a coordinator with a poorly decomposed task list will produce confused delegation no matter how sophisticated its worker agents are.

Core concepts

  • Decomposition granularity (too coarse vs. too fine)
  • Explicit sub-task input/output contracts
  • Dependency ordering between sub-tasks

Real-world example

Breaking "build a landing page" into "write copy," "design layout," and "implement HTML/CSS" — each with a clear contract (copy feeds layout, both feed implementation).

Common mistake

Decomposing tasks too finely, creating so many small pieces that coordination overhead between them exceeds the work saved by parallelizing — an echo of Level 1's exploration vs. exploitation trade-off.

Further reading

  • Classical hierarchical task network (HTN) planning literature

A coordinator agent owns the overall task list and decides which worker agent handles which sub-task and in what order — the role that MetaGPT's SOPs, CrewAI's hierarchical process, and AutoGen's speaker selection all implement in different ways.

Why it matters

This is the first of several specialized agent roles this level covers (workers, reviewers, judges, critics, planners — batch 3 continues this); understanding the coordinator role clearly is the anchor point for all the others.

Core concepts

  • Task-list ownership and dispatch
  • Load balancing across available workers
  • Coordinator as a single point of failure risk

Real-world example

A coordinator that receives "build this feature," decomposes it (per Task Decomposition above), and dispatches sub-tasks to a coding worker, a testing worker, and a documentation worker.

Common mistake

Giving the coordinator no visibility into worker failures, so a stuck or failing worker silently stalls the whole system instead of triggering re-dispatch or escalation.

Further reading

  • Distributed-systems literature on task-queue coordination, applied to agent orchestration

A worker agent executes a single, well-scoped sub-task handed to it by a coordinator — the "doer" role in a multi-agent system, deliberately kept narrow so its behavior is easy to test and reason about in isolation.

Why it matters

System-level reliability comes from workers being narrow and predictable — the coordinator handles the complexity of sequencing and delegation so individual workers don't have to.

Core concepts

  • Narrow scope as a reliability strategy
  • Stateless vs. stateful workers
  • Worker failure reporting back to the coordinator

Real-world example

A "translate this paragraph" worker that does exactly one thing well, called repeatedly by a coordinator across a whole document rather than handling the whole document itself.

Common mistake

Scope creep — letting a worker gradually accumulate extra responsibilities until it's no longer narrow or predictable, undermining the whole reason to separate roles.

Further reading

  • Microservice-design literature on single-responsibility services, applied to agents

A reviewer agent inspects a worker's output against explicit quality standards and either approves it or sends it back with specific, actionable feedback — an evaluator (Level 1) role implemented as a distinct agent rather than folded into the worker itself.

Why it matters

A separate reviewer agent avoids the same blind-spot problem as self-critique (Level 1 — Reflection): a fresh "perspective," even from the same underlying model, catches more than a worker reviewing its own output.

Core concepts

  • Independent review vs. self-review
  • Actionable, specific feedback vs. vague approval/rejection
  • Review criteria as an explicit, checkable rubric

Real-world example

A code-review agent that checks a worker's pull request against a fixed rubric (tests included, no hardcoded secrets, follows style guide) and returns line-specific comments.

Common mistake

Giving a reviewer agent vague criteria ("check if it's good"), which produces inconsistent judgments across runs — the same failure mode covered under Level 2's Reflection Prompts.

Further reading

  • Software code-review best-practice literature, applied to agent review design

A judge agent compares multiple candidate outputs against each other and picks a winner (or ranks them), rather than evaluating a single output against an absolute standard the way a reviewer agent does — the LLM-as-judge pattern implemented as a distinct role.

Why it matters

Relative comparison ("which of these two is better") is often an easier, more reliable judgment for a model to make than absolute scoring ("rate this 1–10"), making judge agents well-suited to selecting among several candidate outputs from a tree- or graph-search loop.

Core concepts

  • Pairwise comparison vs. absolute scoring
  • Position bias in comparative judgments
  • Judge agents as the selection step after tree/graph search

Real-world example

A judge agent picking the best of three candidate email drafts generated in parallel, rather than a single writer agent trying to self-assess its own draft.

Common mistake

Not controlling for position bias — always presenting candidates in the same order can skew a judge agent toward favoring whichever position tends to be judged more favorably.

Further reading

  • Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena" (2023)

A critic agent focuses specifically on finding flaws — it doesn't approve/reject like a reviewer or rank like a judge, it generates a structured list of weaknesses, risks, or counterarguments intended to sharpen a worker's next attempt.

Why it matters

Separating "find problems" (critic) from "decide if it's acceptable" (reviewer) from "pick the best option" (judge) lets each role specialize — a critic optimized purely for finding flaws tends to surface more of them than a role also responsible for a final approve/reject call.

Core concepts

  • Critique generation vs. approval decisions
  • Adversarial critique framing ("argue against this")
  • Structured weakness lists as a critic's output format

Real-world example

A critic agent prompted to "find the three weakest arguments in this essay" before a separate editor agent decides how to address them.

Common mistake

Merging the critic and reviewer roles into one agent, which tends to soften critique — a role that must also approve things is subtly incentivized to find fewer flaws than a role whose only job is finding them.

Further reading

  • Actor-critic literature from reinforcement learning, as a conceptual parallel

A planner agent is the dedicated implementation of Level 1's planning concept and the Plan-and-Execute pattern: given a goal, it produces a sequence of sub-tasks, and is invoked again only when execution reveals the plan needs revising.

Why it matters

Isolating planning into its own agent lets you use a more capable (and more expensive) model just for planning, while cheaper models handle straightforward execution of each step — a cost/capability split that's hard to achieve with one combined agent.

Core concepts

  • Planning as a distinct, callable capability
  • Re-planning triggers and frequency
  • Plan granularity vs. execution flexibility

Real-world example

A planner agent using a strong model to produce a five-step plan once, while a coordinator dispatches each step to cheaper worker agents for execution.

Common mistake

Making plans too granular (specifying exact wording for every step) rather than leaving room for workers to adapt within a step — over-specification defeats the purpose of separating planning from execution.

Further reading

  • See Level 3 — Plan-and-Execute above for the full pattern this role implements

A memory agent owns reading from and writing to a system's persistent memory store — deciding what's worth remembering, retrieving relevant past information for other agents, and pruning what's no longer useful — rather than leaving every agent to manage its own memory ad hoc.

Why it matters

Centralizing memory management in one role prevents the inconsistent, duplicated memory-handling logic that emerges when every agent in a system implements its own version — this is a preview of Level 4's full treatment.

Core concepts

  • Centralized memory read/write ownership
  • Relevance-based retrieval for other agents
  • Preview only — see Level 4 for full memory-loop design

Real-world example

A memory agent that all other agents query for "what have we already tried" instead of each agent maintaining its own separate, potentially inconsistent history.

Common mistake

Skipping a dedicated memory agent in a multi-agent system, leading different agents to have conflicting views of what's already been tried or decided.

Further reading

  • See Level 4 — Memory Loops for the full treatment

A tool agent wraps a specific external capability — a database query, a code execution sandbox, a web search — behind an agent interface, so other agents can request the capability without needing to know its implementation details.

Why it matters

Wrapping tools as agents (rather than raw function calls) lets the tool itself apply judgment — retrying on transient failures, validating inputs, formatting outputs consistently — instead of pushing all of that complexity onto every caller.

Core concepts

  • Tool-agent interface as an abstraction boundary
  • Input validation and output normalization
  • Retry and error handling owned by the tool agent

Real-world example

A "database agent" that other agents query in natural language, which internally handles query construction, retries, and result formatting.

Common mistake

Exposing raw, low-level tool APIs directly to every agent instead of a normalized interface, which spreads tool-specific error handling across the whole system instead of containing it in one place.

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) documentation on standardized tool interfaces

A supervisor agent sits above coordinators, monitoring overall system health — cost, latency, failure rates, loop budgets across the whole system — and can intervene (pause, escalate to a human, kill a runaway sub-loop) independent of any single task's coordinator.

Why it matters

A coordinator manages one task's execution; a supervisor manages the system as a whole, catching failure patterns (like the AutoGPT runaway-loop problem from Batch 1) that no single task-level coordinator would ever see.

Core concepts

  • System-level monitoring vs. task-level coordination
  • Independent intervention authority (pause, kill, escalate)
  • Cross-task budget and cost tracking

Real-world example

A supervisor that notices three separate task coordinators have each independently spawned an unusually large number of sub-tasks in the last hour, and pauses all three pending human review.

Common mistake

Building sophisticated per-task loop budgets (Level 2 — Loop Termination) but no system-level supervisor, leaving no safety net against a whole class of coordinators failing the same way simultaneously.

Further reading

  • See Level 8 — Enterprise Loop Engineering for production monitoring and governance in depth

Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for connecting AI applications with external tools, resources, and prompts through a standardized interface. The July 28, 2026 specification introduced a stateless protocol core, per-request self-description, improved routing, cacheable list results, authorization hardening, first-class extensions, and a formal lifecycle/deprecation policy.

Why it matters

MCP has become an interoperability layer rather than merely a local-tool convenience. A 2026-capable loop engineer needs to understand the current protocol model and the engineering consequences of its shift toward scalable HTTP infrastructure.

Core engineering concepts

  • MCP architecture: hosts, clients, servers, and capability negotiation
  • JSON-RPC request/response model and protocol envelopes
  • Stateless protocol core and per-request metadata
  • Protocol version negotiation and compatibility strategy
  • Tool discovery and tool invocation lifecycle
  • Resources and prompts as distinct MCP primitives
  • MCP server deployment behind ordinary HTTP load balancers
  • Header-based routing using Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name
  • Deterministic list results and cache hints
  • Protocol versioning, deprecation, and migration discipline

Real-world build

Implement a remote MCP server and client against the 2026-07-28 specification, place the server behind a load balancer, cache its tool catalog, and inspect the exact request metadata used for routing and authorization.

Common failure mode

Learning an old session-oriented MCP mental model and carrying deprecated assumptions into new infrastructure, especially sticky-session requirements or legacy transport choices.

Further reading

  • Official MCP specification and July 28, 2026 release notes
  • MCP roadmap and working-group updates
  • MCP SDK documentation for Python/TypeScript/Go/C#

Modern MCP applications expose different kinds of capabilities through tools, resources, prompts, and extensions such as Tasks. Engineering them well requires explicit schemas, predictable semantics, bounded side effects, and clear handling of work that may outlive a single request.

Why it matters

A production agent needs to know not merely that a tool exists, but what contract it exposes, what it can mutate, how it reports errors, and whether work is synchronous or long-running.

Core engineering concepts

  • Tool schemas and JSON Schema 2020-12 compatibility
  • Tool descriptions as machine-readable capability contracts
  • Resources versus tools: data access versus actions
  • Prompts as reusable protocol-level prompt components
  • Task creation, polling, updates, and long-running work
  • Idempotent versus non-idempotent tool operations
  • Side-effect classification and confirmation requirements
  • Error semantics, structured failures, and retry hints
  • Capability discovery and tool catalog hygiene
  • Contract testing for MCP servers and clients

Real-world build

Build an MCP server exposing a read-only resource, a mutating tool, and a long-running Task. Give each a precise schema, explicit side-effect classification, structured errors, and tests for malformed calls.

Common failure mode

Exposing raw backend functions as vague tools with ambiguous inputs, hidden side effects, and no predictable failure contract. The agent then has to guess how the tool behaves.

Further reading

  • MCP 2026-07-28 specification — tools, extensions, Tasks
  • JSON Schema documentation
  • Official MCP SDK examples

The 2026 MCP architecture treats transport as production infrastructure: requests can be routed independently, servers can remain stateless, and capability lists can be cached. This topic focuses on how protocol behavior maps onto gateways, load balancers, caches, and distributed deployments.

Why it matters

Protocol knowledge without infrastructure knowledge is not enough for production agent systems. Stateless routing, cache behavior, and observability determine whether an MCP deployment survives scale and failure.

Core engineering concepts

  • Stateless MCP request handling
  • HTTP transport and request lifecycle
  • Header-based method/name routing
  • Load balancing without sticky protocol sessions
  • Tool-list caching and deterministic result ordering
  • TTL semantics and cache invalidation
  • Gateway authorization based on request metadata
  • Connection failure and retry behavior
  • Latency budgets across agent → gateway → MCP server
  • Tracing protocol requests across distributed infrastructure

Real-world build

Deploy multiple identical MCP server instances behind a reverse proxy. Verify that requests succeed regardless of instance selection, then measure catalog-cache hit rates and end-to-end tool-call latency.

Common failure mode

Assuming protocol sessions must remain pinned to one server instance and accidentally creating a scaling bottleneck that the newer stateless architecture was designed to eliminate.

Further reading

  • MCP July 28, 2026 specification
  • MCP release candidate notes on routable/cacheable transports
  • HTTP load-balancing and distributed-systems references

MCP authorization covers how clients authenticate, how credentials are validated against their issuer, and how enterprise deployments establish managed access across connected servers. The 2026 specification hardens OAuth-aligned behavior and shifts clients toward Client ID Metadata Documents rather than new Dynamic Client Registration deployments.

Why it matters

Agent tool connectivity creates a direct authorization surface. A protocol engineer must understand not only OAuth concepts but how identity, issuer validation, scopes, consent, and credential boundaries interact with agent actions.

Core engineering concepts

  • OAuth 2.x roles and authorization-code style flows in MCP deployments
  • Protected resource metadata and authorization-server discovery
  • Issuer validation and credential binding
  • Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD)
  • Dynamic Client Registration deprecation and compatibility implications
  • Scope design for tool capabilities
  • Enterprise-managed authorization and managed consent
  • Tenant isolation and per-user authorization
  • Secret storage, rotation, and revocation
  • Audit trails linking identities to tool actions

Real-world build

Build an MCP deployment where user identity maps to scoped tool permissions. Test token issuer mismatch, expired credentials, insufficient scopes, tenant boundary violations, and revocation while retaining an auditable action trail.

Common failure mode

Giving an agent a broad credential that effectively bypasses the tool’s intended policy boundary. The protocol may be functioning correctly while the security architecture is still catastrophically permissive.

Further reading

  • MCP 2026-07-28 authorization changes
  • MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization documentation
  • OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect specifications

Agent2Agent is an interoperability protocol for communication between independent agent systems that may use different frameworks, languages, vendors, and internal architectures. Its core model supports capability discovery, interaction-modality negotiation, collaborative tasks, and secure information exchange without requiring agents to reveal their internal memory or tools.

Why it matters

As agent systems become organizations of specialized services rather than single monoliths, interoperable agent-to-agent communication becomes as important as tool interoperability.

Core engineering concepts

  • A2A discovery and agent capability advertisement
  • Agent Cards and machine-readable capability metadata
  • Task-oriented interaction models
  • Conversation/message structures and parts
  • Artifacts and structured outputs
  • Streaming and asynchronous task updates
  • Push notifications and long-running collaboration
  • Authentication and authorization between independent agents
  • Opaque-agent boundaries: communication without shared internal state
  • Protocol versioning and interoperability testing

Real-world build

Build two independent agents using different runtimes: a coordinator delegates a research task to a specialist over A2A, receives asynchronous progress, consumes the resulting artifact, and continues the parent loop without accessing the specialist’s private memory.

Common failure mode

Building “multi-agent” systems that are really tightly coupled function calls with shared hidden state. That destroys portability and makes every agent change cascade through the whole system.

Further reading

  • Official A2A specification — latest released version
  • A2A protocol documentation on Agent Cards and tasks
  • Google/industry documentation on agent interoperability

Agent interoperability engineering combines protocol-level discovery, identity, capability negotiation, task handoff, transport, policy, and observability into a system where independently deployed agents can cooperate without becoming one tightly coupled application.

Why it matters

The important 2026→2027 shift is from “I built several agents” to “I can connect independently owned agents safely.” That requires explicit contracts and trust boundaries between every participating agent.

Core engineering concepts

  • Agent registry and discovery models
  • Capability negotiation and modality negotiation
  • Agent identity and workload identity
  • Task delegation and ownership transfer
  • Contracts for inputs, outputs, artifacts, and errors
  • Inter-agent trust boundaries
  • Policy enforcement at delegation boundaries
  • Protocol gateways and translation layers
  • Cross-agent tracing and correlation IDs
  • Compatibility, contract testing, and graceful degradation

Real-world build

Create a small agent network with a planner, researcher, and executor owned as separate services. Use explicit capability contracts and delegation policies, then simulate one unavailable agent and verify that the coordinator degrades or reroutes instead of stalling the entire system.

Common failure mode

Assuming interoperability means “make the APIs line up.” Real agent interoperability also needs identity, trust, contracts, failure semantics, and observability across service boundaries.

Further reading

  • A2A specification and release notes
  • MCP roadmap — agent communication and identity priorities
  • Distributed systems literature on service contracts and tracing

MCP server architecture covers the lifecycle of a production server: capability declaration, tool/resource/prompt exposure, validation, execution boundaries, error semantics, shutdown, upgrades, and operational health. The protocol contract is only half the design; the server must also behave predictably under failure and change.

Why it matters

Production agent connectivity depends on servers being independently deployable, observable, secure, and upgradeable. A poorly designed MCP server can turn protocol interoperability into a fragile monolith.

Core engineering concepts

  • Server capability discovery
  • Tool/resource/prompt lifecycle
  • Schema validation with JSON Schema
  • Input normalization and output contracts
  • Execution isolation and timeouts
  • Error taxonomy and retry semantics
  • Graceful shutdown and draining
  • Health checks and dependency readiness
  • Backward-compatible capability changes
  • Server versioning and deprecation handling

Real-world build

Implement an MCP server that exposes tools with strict schemas, bounded execution, typed errors, health reporting, and graceful shutdown; deploy two versions and test compatibility.

Common failure mode

Wrapping arbitrary internal functions as tools without contract design, resulting in unstable outputs, leaking implementation details, and unpredictable failure semantics.

Further reading

  • Official MCP specification
  • MCP SDK documentation
  • API contract and service-lifecycle engineering literature

MCP extensions allow the protocol to evolve beyond the core surface while clients and servers explicitly declare support for additional behavior. The engineering task is to negotiate capabilities without making the base integration brittle.

Why it matters

Current MCP development increasingly uses extensions for long-running work, interactive applications, and enterprise capabilities rather than forcing every feature into the protocol core.

Core engineering concepts

  • Extension identifiers and lifecycle
  • Capability advertisement and negotiation
  • Tasks as an extension
  • MCP Apps and server-rendered interaction surfaces
  • Per-request extension signaling
  • Optional versus required capabilities
  • Extension version compatibility
  • Feature detection and graceful fallback
  • Extension security boundaries
  • Testing mixed extension support

Real-world build

Build a client that detects Task support, uses asynchronous work when available, and falls back to ordinary tool calls when the extension is unavailable.

Common failure mode

Assuming every server implements the same optional features and crashing when a capability is absent or changes version.

Further reading

  • MCP 2026-07-28 specification and extensions
  • MCP Apps documentation
  • MCP Tasks extension specification
  • Capability-negotiation patterns in distributed systems

MCP conformance engineering verifies that clients and servers follow protocol schemas, transport behavior, error semantics, authorization requirements, extension contracts, and versioning rules. It turns interoperability from a hope into a testable property.

Why it matters

Agent ecosystems fail at their seams. A server can work perfectly with its own client while violating assumptions made by another implementation.

Core engineering concepts

  • Protocol schema validation
  • Golden request/response fixtures
  • Negative-path and malformed-input testing
  • Transport conformance
  • Capability negotiation tests
  • Authorization-path testing
  • Extension compatibility matrices
  • Cross-SDK interoperability tests
  • Version regression suites
  • Deterministic contract-test environments

Real-world build

Create a conformance harness that runs the same fixture suite against two MCP client/server implementations and reports protocol deviations separately from application-level failures.

Common failure mode

Testing only the happy path. Interoperability bugs frequently live in timeouts, malformed requests, unsupported capabilities, auth failures, and version edges.

Further reading

  • MCP SDK test suites
  • Protocol conformance-testing methodology
  • Contract testing literature

MCP observability makes protocol interactions traceable from agent intent through capability discovery, authorization, tool invocation, server execution, and returned result. Reliability engineering adds bounded retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and recovery semantics around those calls.

Why it matters

Protocol connectivity is distributed-systems connectivity. Without traces and reliable failure semantics, a loop cannot distinguish an agent reasoning failure from a transport or tool-service failure.

Core engineering concepts

  • Request correlation IDs
  • Protocol-level structured logs
  • Latency decomposition
  • Tool execution metrics
  • Timeout and deadline propagation
  • Retry classification and backoff
  • Circuit breakers and bulkheads
  • Partial failure and degraded modes
  • Distributed tracing across agent and server
  • Protocol error versus business-error separation

Real-world build

Instrument an MCP client/server pair with end-to-end traces and intentionally inject latency, dropped connections, and tool failures; verify bounded retries and useful diagnostic traces.

Common failure mode

Retrying every error blindly. This can duplicate side effects, amplify outages, and obscure the original fault.

Further reading

  • MCP protocol diagnostics
  • OpenTelemetry tracing concepts
  • Distributed-systems reliability patterns

A2A discovery gives an agent a machine-readable description of its identity, capabilities, interfaces, skills, authentication requirements, and extensions. Agent Cards make capability discovery explicit before task delegation.

Why it matters

Independent agents cannot safely collaborate when their capabilities and trust requirements are implicit. The current A2A design standardizes discovery and capability description, including well-known Agent Card locations and authenticated extended cards.

Core engineering concepts

  • Agent Card structure
  • Public versus authenticated extended cards
  • Skill and capability advertisement
  • Supported interfaces and protocol versions
  • Well-known agent-card discovery
  • Capability filtering and matching
  • Authentication metadata in discovery
  • Signed Agent Cards and authenticity
  • Caching and refresh of capability metadata
  • Discovery failure and fallback strategies

Real-world build

Build a registry that discovers three specialized agents through Agent Cards, matches a task to the appropriate skill, and refreshes cached capability metadata when versions change.

Common failure mode

Treating discovery documents as static marketing pages rather than security-sensitive machine contracts that influence delegation decisions.

Further reading

  • A2A 1.0 specification
  • A2A Agent Card documentation
  • Service discovery and API registry patterns

A2A task interaction models represent collaborative work that may produce incremental messages, status updates, and artifacts over time. Tasks provide durable logical work units while artifacts represent concrete deliverables.

Why it matters

Agent-to-agent collaboration needs more than request/response text. Long-running work needs task identity, progress semantics, incremental outputs, and a clear completion model. A2A explicitly models Tasks, Artifacts, context identifiers, and streaming updates.

Core engineering concepts

  • Task lifecycle states
  • Context IDs for related work
  • Messages versus durable Tasks
  • Artifact identity and structure
  • Incremental artifact updates
  • Streaming and asynchronous progress
  • Polling and push-notification models
  • Cancellation and failure semantics
  • Task ownership and continuation
  • Mapping protocol tasks to internal workflow state

Real-world build

Build a document-research agent that delegates analysis to a specialist, receives streamed progress, consumes multiple artifacts, and resumes the parent workflow when the specialist completes.

Common failure mode

Encoding an entire multi-step workflow into one opaque message and losing progress, partial artifacts, and cancellation semantics.

Further reading

  • A2A core concepts
  • A2A task lifecycle specification
  • Asynchronous workflow design literature

A2A trust engineering governs whether one independently deployed agent is allowed to invoke another, what it may request, and how the receiving agent authenticates the caller. It treats agent identity as a first-class security boundary rather than trusting network location.

Why it matters

Agent networks create new privilege-escalation paths. A compromised coordinator must not automatically inherit every capability of every downstream agent.

Core engineering concepts

  • Workload identity for agents
  • Authentication schemes declared through Agent Cards
  • Authorization at task/delegation boundaries
  • Audience and issuer validation
  • Capability-scoped credentials
  • Delegation chains and transitive authority
  • Agent impersonation resistance
  • Trust establishment between organizations
  • Auditability of inter-agent actions
  • Revocation and credential rotation

Real-world build

Build two services owned by separate trust domains. Require authenticated A2A calls, scope the delegated capability, log the caller identity, and reject an attempted privilege escalation.

Common failure mode

Confusing “authenticated agent” with “authorized agent.” Successful identity verification does not grant permission to perform every advertised skill.

Further reading

  • A2A security requirements
  • OAuth/OIDC workload identity patterns
  • Zero-trust distributed-system architecture

A2A versioning engineering keeps independently deployed agents interoperable as the protocol evolves. It combines explicit version signaling, interface compatibility, extension negotiation, contract testing, and graceful degradation.

Why it matters

Independent agents cannot be upgraded in lockstep. Current A2A guidance requires explicit protocol-version signaling and provides extension mechanisms so clients and servers can negotiate capabilities without silently assuming compatibility.

Core engineering concepts

  • A2A-Version semantics
  • Major/minor compatibility rules
  • Supported interfaces
  • Extension identifiers and negotiation
  • Backward-compatible Agent Cards
  • Contract and compatibility testing
  • Rolling upgrades across agent fleets
  • Mixed-version deployments
  • Feature detection and fallback
  • Deprecation and migration strategies

Real-world build

Run two A2A agent versions simultaneously behind a gateway. Upgrade the coordinator first, detect unsupported features, and verify that the old specialist continues to operate through a compatibility path.

Common failure mode

Hard-coding one protocol version into every service and discovering incompatibility only after deployment.

Further reading

  • A2A latest specification
  • A2A v1.0 release notes
  • Protocol-versioning and compatibility literature
Level 4

Memory Loops

A full treatment of the concept previewed in Level 1 and touched on by Level 3's memory agent: what a loop-based system remembers, how it stores and retrieves that information, and how it decides what to forget.

Topics: 14 Est. time: ~3.5 hrs Prerequisites: Level 1 (Memory), Level 3 (Memory Agents)

Make the L3 network durable: canonical state, checkpoints, scoped memory, provenance, compaction, schema migration, restart recovery, and auditable deletion become part of the loop.

Why this project exists

A production agent cannot depend on process memory. This project proves that long-lived state survives failures without silently changing meaning or authority.

Builds on the previous level

Persists L3 tasks, artifacts, protocol events, and agent state; keeps identity and policy boundaries intact across recovery.

Architecture flow: Task / Identity → State Store → Checkpoint → Memory Router → Runtime → Recovery Evidence → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • canonical state
  • checkpointing
  • episodic memory
  • semantic memory
  • memory routing
  • provenance
  • compaction
  • schema migration
  • tenant isolation
  • recovery testing
  • deletion lifecycle
  • state replay

Recommended implementation stack

Postgres, Redis/object storage where useful, Python, Pydantic, Docker, pytest, OpenTelemetry

Build sequence

1 · State model

Separate durable task state, working state, memory, artifacts, and telemetry with explicit ownership.

2 · Checkpoint

Persist safe recovery points with version, identity, policy, and schema metadata.

3 · Memory

Implement episodic/semantic stores with ranking, provenance, scope, and retention policies.

4 · Recover

Restart workers mid-task and reconstruct the exact permitted execution context.

5 · Migrate + Delete

Exercise schema migration, memory compaction, revocation, deletion, and tenant isolation.

6 · Package

Publish recovery traces, state diagrams, migration tests, and a chaos report.

Definition of done

  • A worker restart does not lose task correctness.
  • Recovered state preserves identity and policy constraints.
  • Memory has explicit scope and provenance.
  • Schema migrations are tested against old checkpoints.
  • Deletion and retention behavior is demonstrable.
  • Recovery latency and recovery correctness are measured.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • state model
  • checkpoint examples
  • recovery traces
  • migration tests
  • memory provenance
  • chaos report
  • deletion test
  • demo

Public artifact

`durable-agent-memory`: restart-safe agent runtime with memory tiers, checkpoints, and recovery replay.

Project-specific failure to avoid

Persisting chat history while leaving actual task state, authority, and recovery semantics undefined.

Market research basis · 2026

Enterprise agent security guidance increasingly emphasizes runtime identity, traceability, lifecycle governance, and persistent state as core controls rather than optional features.

Portfolio handoff

L5 uses durable state to execute tasks that exceed a single interaction and require replanning.

Short-term memory is the information available to an agent within its current context window — the immediate conversation, recent tool outputs, the current task's state — with no guarantee of surviving beyond the current session.

Why it matters

Nearly all of a loop's per-iteration reasoning draws on short-term memory; understanding its limits (size, decay of attention toward the middle — see Level 1's Context topic) is foundational before adding any longer-term storage.

Core concepts

  • Bounded by the context window
  • Session-scoped — doesn't survive a fresh start
  • Directly equivalent to Level 1's "Context" concept, viewed through a memory lens

Real-world example

An agent recalling a variable name it defined two messages ago in the current conversation, without needing any external storage.

Common mistake

Assuming information mentioned once early in a long session is still salient later — it may technically still be in context but effectively lost to attention decay.

Further reading

  • Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts" (2023)

Long-term memory is information stored outside the context window — in a database, file, or vector store — that an agent can deliberately retrieve when relevant, surviving across sessions and far beyond what any single context window could hold.

Why it matters

It's what turns a series of disconnected sessions into a system that actually accumulates knowledge over time — the Reflexion pattern (Level 3) depends entirely on long-term memory to carry lessons across attempts.

Core concepts

  • External storage outside the context window
  • Deliberate write and retrieve operations
  • Persistence across sessions

Real-world example

An assistant that remembers a user's stated preferences from weeks-old conversations by retrieving them from a persistent store rather than the current context window.

Common mistake

Writing everything to long-term memory indiscriminately, creating a store so noisy that retrieval later surfaces irrelevant results as often as useful ones.

Further reading

  • Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior" (2023) — memory stream design

Vector memory stores information as numeric embeddings and retrieves it by similarity search — finding stored items whose embeddings are closest to a query's embedding — rather than by exact keyword match, letting retrieval work on meaning rather than literal wording.

Why it matters

It's the most common concrete implementation of long-term memory's retrieval step, because it handles paraphrased or conceptually related queries that exact-match search would miss entirely.

Core concepts

  • Embeddings as a numeric representation of meaning
  • Similarity search (nearest-neighbor retrieval)
  • Embedding model choice affects retrieval quality

Real-world example

Retrieving a stored note about "customer was frustrated with slow shipping" when a new query asks about "delivery complaints," despite no shared exact words.

Common mistake

Treating vector similarity as equivalent to relevance — a semantically similar result isn't always the actually useful one for the current task, and pure similarity search can miss that distinction.

Further reading

  • Documentation from vector database providers (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma) on embedding-based retrieval

A knowledge graph stores memory as explicit entities and relationships between them (e.g., "Project X" —depends on→ "Library Y"), enabling structured queries about connections that similarity search over embeddings can't reliably answer.

Why it matters

Vector memory answers "what's similar to this," but knowledge graphs answer "what's connected to this and how" — a different, complementary question that matters for relationship-heavy domains.

Core concepts

  • Entities, relationships, and properties
  • Graph traversal queries vs. similarity queries
  • Combining knowledge graphs with vector memory (hybrid retrieval)

Real-world example

A coding assistant using a knowledge graph of a codebase's module dependencies to answer "what else might break if I change this function" — a question pure similarity search can't answer reliably.

Common mistake

Building and maintaining a knowledge graph for a domain where relationships are sparse or rarely queried, when a simpler vector store would deliver most of the value at a fraction of the maintenance cost.

Further reading

  • Literature on retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge graphs (GraphRAG approaches)

Retrieval is the general act of pulling relevant stored memory back into the current context, whichever storage mechanism (vector, graph, plain database) it comes from — the "read" half of every memory loop's write/read cycle.

Why it matters

Retrieval quality bounds what any downstream reasoning can do — a perfect memory store with poor retrieval is functionally almost as bad as having no memory at all.

Core concepts

  • Query formulation for retrieval
  • Recall vs. precision trade-off in retrieved results
  • Re-ranking retrieved candidates before use

Real-world example

A support agent reformulating a user's vague question into a more specific retrieval query before searching the knowledge base, rather than searching the raw question verbatim.

Common mistake

Retrieving too many results and dumping them all into context unfiltered, reintroducing the context-bloat problem (Level 1 — Context) that memory systems are supposed to help avoid.

Further reading

  • Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (2020)

Memory pruning is the deliberate deletion or deprioritization of stored memories that are outdated, low-value, or redundant — the "forgetting" half of a healthy memory loop, without which a memory store only ever grows and its retrieval quality only ever degrades.

Why it matters

An unpruned memory store accumulates noise and contradictions (an outdated fact stored alongside its later correction), which actively harms retrieval quality over time rather than just costing more storage.

Core concepts

  • Recency and usage-frequency as pruning signals
  • Contradiction detection (newer facts superseding older ones)
  • Soft pruning (deprioritize) vs. hard pruning (delete)

Real-world example

An assistant deprioritizing a stored preference from a year ago in favor of a contradicting preference the user stated last week.

Common mistake

Never pruning at all, on the assumption that "more memory is always better" — in practice, unpruned stores degrade retrieval precision as noise accumulates.

Further reading

  • Park et al., "Generative Agents" (2023) — memory importance and decay scoring

Memory refresh is deliberately re-verifying or updating a stored memory's accuracy over time — checking whether a previously stored fact is still true — rather than treating stored memory as permanently correct once written.

Why it matters

Facts about the world (a person's job, a project's status) change; a memory system that never refreshes drifts further from ground truth the longer it runs.

Core concepts

  • Staleness detection for time-sensitive facts
  • Scheduled vs. triggered refresh
  • Refresh cost vs. staleness risk trade-off

Real-world example

Periodically re-confirming a stored fact like "user's current role" rather than trusting a value that was written six months ago and never revisited.

Common mistake

Refreshing every stored memory on a fixed schedule regardless of how time-sensitive it actually is, wasting effort re-verifying facts that were never going to change.

Further reading

  • Database literature on cache invalidation strategies, as a conceptual parallel

Memory compression applies Level 2's compression concept specifically to long-term storage: reducing many individual memories into fewer, denser ones — turning ten related notes into one consolidated insight — to keep the store itself manageable and retrieval fast.

Why it matters

A memory store that only ever grows eventually becomes expensive to search and prone to burying useful entries among redundant near-duplicates; periodic consolidation keeps it lean.

Core concepts

  • Consolidating related memories into one entry
  • Detecting near-duplicate memories
  • Compression cadence (continuous vs. periodic batch)

Real-world example

Merging ten separate stored notes about a user's food preferences into a single consolidated "dietary preferences" entry.

Common mistake

Compressing too aggressively and losing specific detail that later retrieval needed — the same over-compression risk covered under Level 2's Compression topic, applied to long-term storage.

Further reading

  • See Level 2 — Compression for the general technique this specializes

Memory summarization produces a compact overview of a larger body of stored memory on demand — "summarize everything we know about this customer" — distinct from compression, which permanently reduces the stored memories themselves.

Why it matters

Summarization gives a quick, digestible view without destroying the underlying detail the way permanent compression does — useful when you're not sure yet whether that detail will matter again.

Core concepts

  • On-demand summary generation vs. permanent compression
  • Summarization scope (per-topic, per-session, global)
  • Underlying detail preserved for later retrieval

Real-world example

Generating a one-paragraph "account history" summary for a support agent to read quickly, while the full underlying ticket history remains stored and retrievable separately.

Common mistake

Confusing summarization with compression and discarding the underlying memories after summarizing, losing detail that a future query might have needed.

Further reading

  • Literature on hierarchical and recursive summarization (see Level 2 — Recursive Prompting)

Episodic memory stores specific past events with their context — "on attempt 3, the agent tried X and it failed because Y" — as opposed to general facts. It's the memory type Reflexion (Level 3) relies on to carry lessons from specific past attempts forward.

Why it matters

Episodic memory answers "what happened" questions that general factual memory can't — crucial for any loop that needs to avoid repeating a specific past mistake rather than just knowing general facts about the domain.

Core concepts

  • Event-specific storage with context
  • Time-ordering of episodes
  • Episodic vs. semantic memory distinction

Real-world example

A debugging agent recalling "last Tuesday's deployment failed because of a missing environment variable" as a specific episode, distinct from general knowledge about environment variables.

Common mistake

Storing episodes without enough context to be useful later (just "attempt failed" with no detail on why), which makes the episode nearly worthless when retrieved months later.

Further reading

  • Tulving's original psychological distinction between episodic and semantic memory, as adapted in AI memory system design

Semantic memory stores general facts and concepts, stripped of the specific episode they came from — "the user prefers concise answers" rather than "on March 3rd, the user asked for a shorter response." Knowledge graphs and consolidated preference stores are typically semantic memory.

Why it matters

Semantic memory is usually what should survive compression (Memory Compression above) — the generalized fact is often more durably useful than the specific episode it was first observed in.

Core concepts

  • General facts stripped of episode-specific context
  • Extraction of semantic facts from episodic memory over time
  • Semantic memory as the target of consolidation

Real-world example

After several episodes of a user rejecting long responses, consolidating them into the general semantic fact "prefers concise answers," discarding the specific instances.

Common mistake

Generalizing to a semantic fact from too few episodes, turning a one-off preference into a permanent, over-applied rule.

Further reading

  • Tulving's episodic/semantic memory distinction, as adapted in AI memory system design

Working memory is the small, actively-used subset of information relevant to the current step of a task — narrower than short-term memory's whole context window, it's the handful of facts actually being reasoned over right now.

Why it matters

Explicitly managing working memory (what's the current step actually operating on) rather than leaving it implicit in a sprawling context window improves reasoning focus, echoing Level 1's Context topic at a finer grain.

Core concepts

  • A narrow, actively-used subset of available context
  • Working memory as the "current focus" within short-term memory
  • Explicit scoping to reduce distraction from irrelevant context

Real-world example

An agent working through a multi-step math problem keeping only the current sub-expression and running total "in working memory" instead of re-deriving from the full problem statement each step.

Common mistake

Letting working memory silently expand to include everything in the context window, which defeats the purpose of scoping it narrowly to the current step.

Further reading

  • Cognitive-science literature on working memory capacity limits, as a conceptual parallel

Persistent memory is long-term memory's implementation concern: the actual durable storage layer (a database, file system, or managed service) that survives process restarts, deployments, and infrastructure changes — the "how" behind long-term memory's "what."

Why it matters

A memory design can be conceptually sound (right pruning rules, right compression strategy) and still fail in production if the underlying persistence layer isn't actually durable, backed up, and available when needed.

Core concepts

  • Durability guarantees of the storage layer
  • Backup and recovery for memory stores
  • Consistency across concurrent reads/writes from multiple agents

Real-world example

Choosing a managed vector database with automatic backups over an in-memory store that would silently lose all memory on a service restart.

Common mistake

Prototyping a memory system with in-process storage and deploying it to production unchanged, discovering only after the first restart that all accumulated memory was lost.

Further reading

  • See Level 8 — Enterprise Loop Engineering for production data-reliability practices
Level 5

Evaluation Loops

The full treatment of the concept introduced in Level 1 and leaned on throughout Levels 2–4: how to build the "sensor" that tells a loop whether it's actually improving, and how to trust that sensor at production scale.

Topics: 14 Est. time: ~3.5 hrs Prerequisites: Level 1 (Evaluation)

Build a persistent planner that executes a 20–50 step task through dependency graphs, milestones, checkpoints, progress evaluation, replanning, budget control, stuck-state detection, and human escalation.

Why this project exists

Long-horizon work exposes failure modes that short demos hide: drift, compounding errors, dead ends, budget exhaustion, and false completion.

Builds on the previous level

Consumes L4 durable state and memory; every plan revision and checkpoint is persisted and evaluated.

Architecture flow: Objective → Task Graph → Scheduler → Workers / Tools → Progress Evaluator → Replan + Escalate → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • task decomposition
  • dependency graphs
  • milestones
  • progress estimation
  • replanning
  • stuck-state detection
  • budget control
  • checkpointing
  • trajectory evaluation
  • human escalation
  • partial-credit evaluation
  • plan versioning

Recommended implementation stack

Python, workflow/runtime framework, Postgres, Redis/queue, pytest, OpenTelemetry, evaluation harness

Build sequence

1 · Define task

Choose a 20–50 step benchmark with explicit success criteria, dependencies, budgets, and partial credit.

2 · Plan

Generate a versioned task graph with milestones and preconditions.

3 · Execute

Run workers with durable checkpoints and bounded concurrency.

4 · Evaluate

Score intermediate progress and detect drift, stuck states, false completion, and wasted actions.

5 · Replan

Revise the plan without destroying useful state; escalate when authority or budget boundaries are reached.

6 · Package

Publish trajectory traces, plan versions, recovery examples, and a quantitative benchmark.

Definition of done

  • The benchmark runs for at least 20 meaningful steps.
  • At least three injected failures trigger recovery or escalation.
  • Plan revisions are versioned and explainable.
  • Budget exhaustion produces controlled termination.
  • Progress is evaluated before final completion.
  • A trajectory report compares baseline and improved policies.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • task benchmark
  • plan graph
  • trajectory traces
  • replan diff
  • failure matrix
  • budget report
  • eval results
  • demo

Public artifact

`long-horizon-loop`: durable 20–50 step benchmark with plan/version viewer and trajectory evaluator.

Project-specific failure to avoid

Calling a multi-step chain “long horizon” when it has no persistent state, intermediate evaluation, or recovery.

Market research basis · 2026

2026 production-agent research increasingly distinguishes agent capability from production readiness; quality, observability, and evaluation remain central gaps.

Portfolio handoff

L6 gives the long-horizon system a real external environment to operate in.

LLM evaluation is the umbrella discipline of measuring a language model's outputs against some standard of quality — spanning capability benchmarks, task-specific correctness, and subjective quality judgments — as opposed to evaluating traditional software, which usually has unambiguous pass/fail tests.

Why it matters

LLM outputs are often open-ended and don't have a single correct answer, which means evaluation itself needs deliberate design — it's rarely as simple as "does the output match the expected value."

Core concepts

  • Open-ended vs. closed-form evaluation tasks
  • Capability benchmarks vs. task-specific evaluation
  • The evaluation-design problem as distinct from the task itself

Real-world example

Evaluating a summarization model requires judging fluency, factual accuracy, and completeness together — no single metric captures all three, unlike checking whether a sort function produced a sorted list.

Common mistake

Treating LLM evaluation like traditional unit testing and expecting a single deterministic pass/fail signal for inherently open-ended tasks.

Further reading

  • Chang et al., "A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models" (2023)

Human evaluation has real people directly judge outputs — the gold-standard signal for subjective quality, but slow and expensive relative to automated methods, which makes it best reserved for calibrating automated evaluators rather than gating every loop iteration.

Why it matters

Every automated evaluator (LLM-as-judge, metrics) is only as good as its agreement with human judgment — human evaluation is what validates that the cheaper, faster automated signal is actually trustworthy.

Core concepts

  • Human evaluation as ground truth for calibrating automation
  • Inter-rater agreement and rubric design
  • Sampling strategy (evaluating a subset, not every output)

Real-world example

Periodically having human raters score a random sample of an LLM-judge's decisions to confirm the judge still agrees with human preferences as the underlying model changes.

Common mistake

Using human evaluation as the only evaluation signal in a tight iteration loop, which makes the loop far too slow and expensive to actually run at the frequency needed.

Further reading

  • Human-evaluation rubric design practices from major LLM provider research blogs

Automatic evaluation uses code, not human or model judgment, to check outputs — exact-match comparisons, regex checks, unit tests, schema validation — anywhere a deterministic, objective check is possible.

Why it matters

It's the fastest, cheapest, and most reliable evaluation signal available, and should always be preferred over LLM-as-judge or human evaluation wherever a task's success can actually be checked deterministically.

Core concepts

  • Deterministic checks (exact match, regex, schema validation)
  • Unit and integration tests as an evaluation signal
  • Where automatic checks stop being sufficient

Real-world example

Validating that a model's JSON output parses correctly and matches a required schema, entirely in code, with no judgment call needed.

Common mistake

Reaching for LLM-as-judge on tasks that actually have a deterministic correctness check available — this is slower, costlier, and less reliable than the automatic check would have been.

Further reading

  • Standard software testing literature, applied to LLM output validation

LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to evaluate outputs where neither automatic checks nor human evaluation are practical at the needed scale and speed — the full evaluation-focused treatment of Level 3's Judge Agent role.

Why it matters

It occupies the useful middle ground between automatic evaluation (fast but limited to checkable tasks) and human evaluation (accurate but slow and expensive) — the workhorse evaluator for most subjective quality loops.

Core concepts

  • Judge prompt design and rubric specification
  • Position bias and length bias in judge outputs
  • Calibrating judge agreement against human evaluation

Real-world example

An LLM judge scoring 500 chatbot responses per day for helpfulness and tone, at a fraction of the cost and time of having humans review each one.

Common mistake

Deploying an LLM judge without first validating its agreement rate against human judgments — an uncalibrated judge can systematically favor certain styles (e.g., longer answers) regardless of actual quality.

Further reading

  • Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena" (2023)

Metrics are the specific numeric measures a loop tracks — accuracy, F1 score, ROUGE for summarization, task-completion rate — chosen to approximate the true objective (Level 1) in a form that's cheap to compute repeatedly.

Why it matters

Every metric is a proxy, never the objective itself; picking metrics that correlate poorly with what actually matters is the most common root cause of loops that "improve the number" without improving real quality.

Core concepts

  • Metric as proxy for objective
  • Task-specific metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, exact match, etc.)
  • Composite metrics combining multiple signals

Real-world example

Tracking both "response length" and "user satisfaction rating" together, because length alone can be gamed without actually improving satisfaction.

Common mistake

Optimizing a single easy-to-measure metric in isolation — directly connected to Level 1's warning about proxy objectives and Goodhart's Law.

Further reading

  • Lin, "ROUGE: A Package for Automatic Evaluation of Summaries" (2004)

A benchmark is a standardized, fixed set of tasks with known expected behavior used to compare systems (or versions of the same system) consistently over time — the system-level counterpart to Level 2's prompt benchmarking, scoped to entire agents or pipelines.

Why it matters

Standardized benchmarks are what make "model B is better than model A at task X" a checkable claim rather than an impression — essential for comparing systems across teams or over time.

Core concepts

  • Public benchmarks vs. private/internal benchmarks
  • Benchmark contamination (test data leaking into training)
  • Benchmark saturation over time

Real-world example

Maintaining an internal benchmark of 200 real customer queries to compare agent versions consistently, since public benchmarks may not reflect this company's actual traffic.

Common mistake

Relying solely on public, widely-known benchmarks that models may have been directly or indirectly trained toward, inflating scores relative to real-world performance.

Further reading

  • Documentation for widely used benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K) and their known limitations

Regression testing re-runs a fixed benchmark after any change — a prompt edit, a model version update, a new tool — to catch cases where something that used to work now fails, before that change reaches production.

Why it matters

LLM systems can regress in subtle, non-obvious ways when anything upstream changes; without regression testing, these regressions are typically discovered by users in production rather than caught before deployment.

Core concepts

  • Fixed regression suite run before every change
  • Regression thresholds (how much drop is acceptable)
  • Regression testing across model version upgrades specifically

Real-world example

Automatically re-running a 100-case regression suite whenever a production prompt template changes, blocking deployment if scores drop below a set threshold.

Common mistake

Only testing new functionality when making a change, without re-verifying that previously working cases still pass.

Further reading

  • Standard software regression-testing practice, applied to prompt and model version changes

Hallucination detection identifies confidently stated but factually incorrect or unsupported claims in a model's output — a specialized evaluation problem because hallucinations are often fluent and plausible-sounding, making them hard to catch without external verification.

Why it matters

As covered in Level 0's misconceptions, a model reflecting on its own hallucination often just re-confirms it — reliable hallucination detection almost always requires an external source of truth, not more self-critique.

Core concepts

  • Fact-checking against external, retrieved sources
  • Claim extraction and per-claim verification
  • Confidence-calibration mismatches as a hallucination signal

Real-world example

Extracting individual factual claims from a generated summary and checking each against the source document it was supposed to summarize, rather than trusting the summary's fluent tone.

Common mistake

Using fluency or confidence of tone as a proxy for accuracy — hallucinated content is often stated just as confidently and fluently as accurate content.

Further reading

  • Huang et al., "A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models" (2023)

Safety evaluation specifically checks for harmful, unsafe, or policy-violating outputs — a distinct evaluation dimension from general quality, since an output can be fluent and helpful- sounding while still being unsafe.

Why it matters

Safety and quality don't always correlate — a loop optimized purely for helpfulness or engagement metrics can drift toward unsafe outputs unless safety is evaluated as its own explicit dimension.

Core concepts

  • Safety as a separate evaluation axis from quality
  • Red-teaming as an adversarial evaluation method
  • Guardrails (Level 3) as safety evaluation running in production

Real-world example

Running a suite of adversarial prompts specifically designed to probe for unsafe outputs, separate from the normal quality benchmark suite.

Common mistake

Assuming a high quality score implies safety — the two are measuring genuinely different things and both need dedicated evaluation.

Further reading

  • Anthropic's and other major labs' published safety-evaluation and red-teaming methodologies

Quality scoring combines multiple evaluation signals — metrics, LLM-judge ratings, safety checks — into a single score (or small set of scores) that a loop can act on directly, typically via an explicit weighted formula rather than an ad-hoc combination.

Why it matters
