A loop's termination and decision-making steps (Level 1, 2) usually need one actionable number, not five separate signals to reconcile manually every iteration — quality scoring is where that reconciliation happens deliberately.

Core concepts

  • Weighted combination of multiple evaluation signals
  • Explicit weighting vs. black-box combined scores
  • Score interpretability for debugging

Real-world example

Combining a 40% weight on factual accuracy, 30% on tone match, and 30% on length compliance into one overall score that a refinement loop's termination rule checks against a threshold.

Common mistake

Using opaque weightings that make it hard to tell why a given output scored low — an interpretable score breakdown matters as much as the score itself for debugging a stuck loop.

Further reading

  • Multi-criteria decision analysis literature, applied to composite quality scores

Performance monitoring tracks evaluation signals continuously in production, not just during development — turning evaluation from a one-time pre-launch check into an ongoing loop that can catch quality drift as real-world traffic and usage patterns shift over time.

Why it matters

A system that scored well in offline evaluation can still degrade in production as input distributions shift — ongoing monitoring is what catches this, since offline benchmarks alone can't.

Core concepts

  • Continuous vs. one-time evaluation
  • Alerting on quality-metric degradation
  • Sampling production traffic for ongoing evaluation

Real-world example

Sampling 5% of production responses daily for LLM-judge scoring, and alerting the team if average quality drops below a set threshold for two consecutive days.

Common mistake

Treating evaluation as a pre-launch gate only, with no ongoing production monitoring — this is preview material for Level 8's full enterprise monitoring treatment.

Further reading

  • See Level 8 — Enterprise Loop Engineering for full production observability

Cost optimization treats compute spend as an evaluation dimension in its own right — tracking cost per loop iteration, per completed task, or per unit of quality gained — so decisions about loop budgets (Level 2) are grounded in actual numbers rather than intuition.

Why it matters

Loops multiply cost by design (that's the trade-off Level 0 describes); without deliberate cost tracking, it's easy to build a loop that's technically effective but economically unviable at scale.

Core concepts

  • Cost per iteration and cost per completed task
  • Marginal quality gained per additional dollar spent
  • Model-tier selection as a cost/quality lever

Real-world example

Measuring that a loop's fourth refinement attempt improves quality by only 2%, at the same cost as the first attempt's 20% improvement, and setting the loop budget accordingly.

Common mistake

Optimizing purely for quality with no cost visibility, discovering the loop's per-task economics don't work only after it's already in production at scale.

Further reading

  • See Level 8 — Enterprise Loop Engineering for production cost management practices

Latency optimization measures and reduces how long a loop takes to converge — end-to-end wall-clock time, not just iteration count — since a loop that's cheap in compute but slow in real time can still be unusable for latency-sensitive applications.

Why it matters

Cost and latency are related but distinct: parallelizing independent evaluation calls, for instance, can cut latency without changing total cost — evaluating both separately opens optimization options neither alone would reveal.

Core concepts

  • Wall-clock latency vs. total compute cost
  • Parallelizable vs. inherently sequential loop steps
  • Latency budgets for user-facing loops

Real-world example

Running a tree-prompting loop's sibling-branch evaluations in parallel rather than sequentially, cutting wall-clock time substantially at the same total compute cost.

Common mistake

Optimizing only for cost or only for quality and treating latency as an afterthought, then discovering a technically excellent loop is too slow for its actual use case.

Further reading

  • See Level 8 — Enterprise Loop Engineering for production latency and scaling practices
Level 6

Coding Loops

Software engineering is where loop engineering is most mature in practice — this level applies every earlier concept (planning, evaluation, agent roles, memory) to the specific, well-understood domain of writing and shipping code.

Topics: 12 Est. time: ~3 hrs Prerequisites: Level 1, Level 3, Level 5

Extend L5 into a sandboxed computer-use environment where the agent grounds screenshots/DOM state, proposes actions, passes an action gate, executes in isolation, verifies postconditions, and recovers from UI drift.

Why this project exists

Computer-use exposes the gap between abstract tool calls and messy environments: state changes, untrusted content, credentials, UI drift, and irreversible actions.

Builds on the previous level

Uses L5 planning, checkpoints, trajectory evaluation, and escalation; computer actions become durable tool events.

Architecture flow: Task + Plan → UI Grounding → Action Gate → Sandbox → Observation → Verifier + Replay → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • visual grounding
  • DOM/accessibility grounding
  • action primitives
  • browser state
  • session isolation
  • sandboxing
  • credential handoff
  • UI drift handling
  • irreversible-action gates
  • postcondition verification
  • trajectory replay
  • environment reset

Recommended implementation stack

Playwright/browser automation, isolated container or VM, Python/TypeScript, screenshot capture, policy engine, tracing

Build sequence

1 · Sandbox

Create reproducible browser/desktop environments with resettable state and no ambient credentials.

2 · Ground

Represent screenshots, DOM/accessibility state, and targets in a common observation schema.

3 · Gate

Classify actions by risk and require policy/human approval for sensitive operations.

4 · Execute

Perform clicks, typing, navigation, uploads, downloads, and waits with bounded retries.

5 · Break

Inject UI drift, malicious pages, stale selectors, session expiry, and ambiguous targets.

6 · Package

Publish replayable trajectories, environment snapshots, security boundaries, and demo video.

Definition of done

  • The environment resets to a known state.
  • Sensitive actions are gated before execution.
  • Credentials are not exposed to untrusted page content.
  • UI drift produces recovery rather than blind repetition.
  • Every action has before/after evidence.
  • A failed trajectory can be replayed.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • environment spec
  • action policy
  • trajectory replay
  • UI drift cases
  • sandbox test
  • credential boundary
  • demo
  • threat note

Public artifact

`computer-use-workbench`: reproducible browser environment with action gating and trajectory replay.

Project-specific failure to avoid

A browser automation script that succeeds on one page state but has no sandbox, policy gate, or recovery evidence.

Market research basis · 2026

2026 agent security research highlights the risks of agents operating with private data, untrusted content, and outbound action capability; computer use therefore needs explicit isolation and action governance.

Portfolio handoff

L7 attacks every layer built so far and turns observed weaknesses into enforceable controls.

Spec generation turns an informal request ("add search to the app") into an explicit, checkable specification — inputs, outputs, edge cases, constraints — before any code is written, giving the rest of the coding loop an objective (Level 1) to evaluate against.

Why it matters

A coding loop without a spec has no way to distinguish "done and correct" from "done and technically running" — the spec is what makes automatic evaluation (Level 5) possible at all.

Core concepts

  • Explicit inputs, outputs, and edge cases
  • Spec as the evaluation objective for the rest of the loop
  • Ambiguity resolution before implementation starts

Real-world example

Turning "add search" into "given a query string, return matching items ranked by relevance, case-insensitive, with empty-query and no-match cases explicitly handled."

Common mistake

Skipping explicit spec generation for "simple" tasks, only to discover disagreement about correct edge-case behavior after implementation is already underway.

Further reading

  • Software requirements engineering literature on specification practices

Coding-specific planning applies Level 1's planning concept and Level 3's Plan-and-Execute pattern to software: deciding which files to touch, in what order, and how changes decompose into independently testable pieces — before writing the first line.

Why it matters

A coding agent that plans file-by-file changes up front can parallelize independent work and re-plan just the affected part when a step fails, rather than re-deriving the whole approach after every setback.

Core concepts

  • File- and module-level change decomposition
  • Dependency ordering between changes
  • Re-planning scope after a failed step

Real-world example

Planning "update the data model, then the API layer, then the UI" in that order because each step depends on the previous one being correct.

Common mistake

Diving straight into implementation on a multi-file change without an explicit plan, leading to inconsistent intermediate states across files.

Further reading

  • See Level 1 — Planning and Level 3 — Plan-and-Execute for the general patterns this specializes

Implementation is the "generate" step of the coding loop: given a spec and a plan, producing actual code — the part most people think of as "coding," but only one of several steps that together determine whether a change actually works.

Why it matters

In loop engineering terms, implementation quality matters far less in isolation than the loop around it — a mediocre first implementation caught and fixed by a strong testing/review loop beats a "perfect" first attempt with no verification.

Core concepts

  • Implementation as one step in a larger loop, not the whole loop
  • Incremental implementation vs. large batch changes
  • Implementation scoped tightly to the spec

Real-world example

Implementing one function at a time and running its specific tests before moving to the next, rather than writing an entire feature before any verification.

Common mistake

Treating implementation as the only step that matters and under-investing in the surrounding testing and review loop that actually catches most real defects.

Further reading

  • General software-engineering literature on incremental development

Testing is coding's clearest example of Level 5's automatic evaluation: a test suite gives a deterministic, ground-truth pass/fail signal that a coding loop can trust far more than self-assessment of whether code "looks correct."

Why it matters

A coding agent looping against a real test suite is structurally more reliable than one looping against its own judgment of correctness — it's the single clearest real-world case of Level 5's "prefer automatic evaluation where possible" principle.

Core concepts

  • Tests as ground-truth evaluation for a coding loop
  • Test coverage vs. test quality
  • Writing tests before or alongside implementation

Real-world example

A coding agent that writes both the implementation and its tests, then loops on the implementation until the independently-written tests pass.

Common mistake

Letting the same generation pass write both the code and tests that are subtly shaped to pass that specific code, which can mask real bugs rather than catching them.

Further reading

  • Test-driven development literature, as applied to agent-driven coding loops

Debugging is the coding domain's error correction (Level 1) step: given a failing test, isolating the root cause and applying a targeted fix — the specific skill that determines whether a coding loop actually converges or just keeps producing new failures.

Why it matters

Debugging quality is the coding loop's bottleneck far more often than implementation quality — a strong debugger converges in two or three iterations; a weak one can loop indefinitely without making real progress.

Core concepts

  • Reproducing the failure reliably before attempting a fix
  • Root-cause isolation from a stack trace or test failure
  • Targeted fixes vs. symptom patching (Level 1 — Error Correction)

Real-world example

An agent reading a stack trace, forming a hypothesis about the specific line causing the failure, and verifying that hypothesis with a minimal reproduction before editing.

Common mistake

Making speculative changes without first reproducing and understanding the failure — this often "fixes" the visible symptom while leaving the actual bug in place.

Further reading

  • See Level 1 — Error Correction for the general pattern this specializes

Code review is the coding domain's implementation of Level 3's Reviewer Agent role: inspecting a change against standards tests alone don't check — readability, maintainability, security, architectural fit — and approving or requesting changes.

Why it matters

Passing tests proves a change works for the cases tested; it doesn't prove the change is maintainable, secure, or architecturally sound — review catches the class of problems automatic evaluation structurally can't.

Core concepts

  • Review dimensions beyond correctness (security, style, architecture)
  • Structured review rubrics (Level 3 — Reviewer Agents)
  • Human-in-the-loop review vs. automated review agents

Real-world example

A review agent flagging that a passing implementation hardcodes a credential, even though no test caught it — a security concern outside what the test suite checks.

Common mistake

Treating "all tests pass" as equivalent to "ready to merge," skipping review dimensions that tests were never designed to catch.

Further reading

  • See Level 3 — Reviewer Agents for the general role this specializes

Refactoring restructures existing code without changing its external behavior — a loop whose evaluation signal is "tests still pass and the code is now better by some quality measure," distinct from feature loops where the goal is new behavior.

Why it matters

Refactoring loops need the test suite to already be trustworthy — a weak test suite means "tests still pass" doesn't actually guarantee behavior was preserved, which is the whole point of the loop.

Core concepts

  • Behavior-preservation as the core evaluation constraint
  • Test-suite trustworthiness as a prerequisite
  • Incremental refactoring vs. large rewrites

Real-world example

An agent simplifying a tangled function's control flow one small step at a time, re-running the full test suite after each step to confirm behavior hasn't changed.

Common mistake

Attempting a large, sweeping refactor in one pass rather than many small, independently-verified steps, making it hard to isolate which change (if any) broke something.

Further reading

  • Fowler, "Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code"

CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) is the historical loop mentioned back in Level 0: build, test, deploy, monitor, fix, repeat — largely automated infrastructure that a coding agent's own inner loop now plugs into rather than replaces.

Why it matters

A coding agent's local edit-test-fix loop and the organization's CI/CD pipeline are nested loops at different scales — understanding the boundary between them clarifies what an agent should verify itself versus what the pipeline will catch anyway.

Core concepts

  • Build, test, deploy, monitor, fix as pipeline stages
  • Local agent loop vs. pipeline-level loop
  • Fast local feedback vs. slower full-pipeline feedback

Real-world example

A coding agent running a fast local subset of tests before committing, trusting the full CI pipeline to catch anything its local loop didn't have time to check.

Common mistake

Relying entirely on the (slow) CI pipeline as the only feedback loop, instead of running a fast local subset first — this makes every iteration far more expensive than necessary.

Further reading

  • See Level 0 — History for CI/CD's role in loop engineering's lineage

Regression loops apply Level 5's regression testing specifically to code: automatically running the full test suite against every proposed change and blocking merge on any newly-failing test, closing the loop between "code changed" and "did anything break."

Why it matters

Without an automated regression loop, catching a broken previously-working feature depends on someone manually noticing — automating it turns detection from reactive to immediate.

Core concepts

  • Full-suite re-run on every change
  • Merge-blocking on regression detection
  • Flaky-test handling (distinguishing real regressions from noise)

Real-world example

A pull request automatically blocked from merging because it broke a previously-passing test in an unrelated module, catching an unintended side effect before it reached production.

Common mistake

Letting flaky (inconsistently passing) tests erode trust in the regression loop, to the point where failures get ignored or overridden rather than investigated.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Regression Testing for the general evaluation pattern this specializes

A code agent composes every topic in this level — spec generation, planning, implementation, testing, debugging, review — into one working system, using ReAct-style tool use (Level 3) to read files, run commands, and iterate until the spec is met.

Why it matters

Coding agents are one of the most mature production applications of loop engineering precisely because the domain has strong automatic evaluation (tests) — the loop's "sensor" problem is largely solved, which most other domains in this roadmap don't have as cleanly.

Core concepts

  • Composition of the full coding-loop stack into one agent
  • Tool use for file editing, command execution, and test running
  • Why coding is an unusually favorable domain for agent loops

Real-world example

Claude Code running plan → edit → test → fix cycles autonomously within a repository, using real test results as its evaluation signal at every step.

Common mistake

Assuming success with a coding agent transfers directly to domains lacking coding's strong automatic evaluation — the same loop design can perform very differently where the evaluation signal is weaker.

Further reading

  • Documentation and engineering blog posts from major coding-agent products

Developer workflows are how coding loops integrate into how humans actually work — where a human reviews before merge, where an agent runs fully autonomously, where a human needs to approve a plan before execution begins — the human-in-the-loop design question applied to software teams specifically.

Why it matters

The best coding loop design is worthless if it doesn't fit how the team actually ships software — workflow integration determines whether a well-built agent loop gets adopted or abandoned.

Core concepts

  • Human approval gates within the loop
  • Autonomous vs. supervised execution modes
  • Fitting agent loops into existing team processes (PRs, sprints)

Real-world example

A team requiring human approval of an agent's plan before execution begins, but letting the edit-test-fix loop within an approved plan run autonomously.

Common mistake

Designing an agent loop in isolation from how the team actually reviews and ships code, producing a technically sound system nobody integrates into daily use.

Further reading

  • Engineering-productivity research on developer tool adoption patterns
Level 7

Research Loops

Where coding loops benefit from strong automatic evaluation (tests), research loops face the opposite challenge: truth itself is often what's being sought, which makes evaluation the central, hardest problem in this level.

Topics: 10 Est. time: ~2.5 hrs Prerequisites: Level 1, Level 5

Build a red-team laboratory that systematically attacks the L0–L6 stack across prompt/context, memory, tools, identity, protocols, computer environments, and runtime state, then converts findings into deterministic controls.

Why this project exists

Security is not a final checklist. The portfolio must prove that you can discover agent-specific attack paths, measure blast radius, preserve evidence, and close the loop with mitigations.

Builds on the previous level

Imports L0–L6 fixtures and deliberately attacks their contracts, state, tool gateways, protocol boundaries, and computer-use environment.

Architecture flow: Attack Generator → Untrusted Input → Agent Stack → Policy / Sandbox → Telemetry → Incident + Fix Loop → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • agent threat modeling
  • prompt injection
  • context poisoning
  • tool poisoning
  • identity abuse
  • least privilege
  • MCP/A2A abuse
  • memory poisoning
  • sandbox escape testing
  • data exfiltration tests
  • incident response
  • security regression testing

Recommended implementation stack

Python, isolated Docker/VM environments, proxy/policy gateway, pytest, fuzzing, trace store, security test harness

Build sequence

1 · Model

Map assets, identities, trust boundaries, attack surfaces, blast radius, and recovery assumptions.

2 · Generate

Create deterministic attack fixtures for injection, poisoning, tool abuse, identity misuse, and memory corruption.

3 · Execute

Run attacks against the portfolio stack inside disposable environments.

4 · Detect

Correlate traces, policy decisions, identity, tool calls, and state changes into incidents.

5 · Contain + Fix

Quarantine, revoke, reset, patch, and add regression tests for every accepted finding.

6 · Package

Publish a threat model, attack corpus, severity matrix, remediation report, and red-team demo.

Definition of done

  • Every major trust boundary has at least one attack test.
  • Successful attacks produce a reproducible fixture and evidence trail.
  • Containment actions are tested, not merely described.
  • Security fixes become regression tests.
  • Blast radius is quantified for at least three attack classes.
  • The final report distinguishes residual from mitigated risk.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • threat model
  • attack corpus
  • trace evidence
  • severity matrix
  • remediation diff
  • regression suite
  • incident report
  • demo

Public artifact

`adversarial-agent-lab`: reproducible agent attack corpus + containment harness + security regression suite.

Project-specific failure to avoid

A list of prompt-injection examples with no threat model, runtime evidence, containment, or regression testing.

A literature review loop searches, filters, and organizes existing sources on a topic — iteratively refining search terms based on what earlier searches turned up, rather than a single fixed query, until the space of relevant prior work is adequately covered.

Why it matters

A single search rarely surfaces a topic's full relevant literature; the loop's refine step — reformulating queries based on terminology and citations found in early results — is what actually achieves reasonable coverage.

Core concepts

  • Iterative query refinement based on prior results
  • Coverage vs. precision trade-off in search
  • Citation chaining (following references to find more sources)

Real-world example

A research agent that, after an initial search, notices a recurring technical term in top results and runs a follow-up search specifically on that term.

Common mistake

Stopping after one search pass and treating the results as comprehensive, missing significant work that used different terminology than the initial query.

Further reading

  • Systematic-review methodology literature from evidence-based research practice

Hypothesis generation proposes candidate explanations or claims worth investigating — an abductive-reasoning task (Level 1) applied to open questions, where the loop's job is producing testable hypotheses, not yet confirming them.

Why it matters

Good hypothesis generation focuses the far more expensive evidence-collection and verification steps that follow — a vague or untestable hypothesis wastes downstream effort no matter how well those later steps are executed.

Core concepts

  • Testable vs. untestable hypotheses
  • Hypothesis specificity as a quality signal
  • Generating multiple competing hypotheses (Level 3 — Tree/Graph exploration)

Real-world example

Given an unexplained drop in a metric, generating several specific, checkable hypotheses ("a deploy on date X caused it," "seasonal effect") rather than one vague guess.

Common mistake

Generating hypotheses too vague to actually test ("something changed in user behavior"), which gives the verification step nothing concrete to check.

Further reading

  • See Level 1 — Reasoning for abductive reasoning as the underlying mechanism

Evidence collection gathers information relevant to a specific hypothesis — targeted retrieval, distinct from the broader literature review — with each piece of evidence tagged as supporting, contradicting, or neutral toward the hypothesis being investigated.

Why it matters

Evidence collection that only searches for confirming information produces confirmation bias baked into the loop itself; deliberately searching for contradicting evidence too is what makes the loop's conclusion trustworthy.

Core concepts

  • Hypothesis-targeted vs. general-purpose search
  • Confirming vs. contradicting evidence tagging
  • Evidence quality assessment (source reliability)

Real-world example

A research agent deliberately searching for counterexamples to a hypothesis, not just supporting cases, before concluding the hypothesis is well-supported.

Common mistake

Only searching for evidence that confirms the hypothesis already favored, systematically missing contradicting evidence — a research-specific version of Level 5's hallucination-detection blind-spot problem.

Further reading

  • Literature on confirmation bias in research methodology

Verification weighs collected evidence to determine whether a hypothesis is supported, refuted, or still uncertain — the research loop's evaluation step, and its hardest one, since unlike coding's test suite there's rarely a single definitive check.

Why it matters

This is where research loops most need external grounding (Level 0's misconceptions) rather than self-assessment — a model judging its own hypothesis as verified is exactly the self-critique blind-spot pattern to avoid.

Core concepts

  • Weighing evidence quality, not just quantity
  • Degrees of confidence rather than binary verified/refuted
  • External verification vs. self-assessment

Real-world example

Concluding a hypothesis is "moderately supported" with three corroborating sources and one unresolved contradiction, rather than declaring it definitively true.

Common mistake

Treating "found supporting evidence" as equivalent to "verified" — a hypothesis can have supporting evidence and still be wrong if contradicting evidence wasn't adequately weighed.

Further reading

  • See Level 0 — Common Misconceptions for the self-verification blind-spot this echoes

Fact checking is verification applied to individual, discrete claims — narrower than hypothesis verification, it's the research-domain instance of Level 5's hallucination detection: checking a specific stated fact against a reliable source.

Why it matters

Research outputs often mix well-supported synthesis with individual unverified claims — fact checking at the claim level catches errors that a whole-document quality check would average over and miss.

Core concepts

  • Claim extraction from a larger text
  • Per-claim source verification
  • Distinguishing checkable facts from opinions or interpretations

Real-world example

Extracting every numeric claim from a draft report and individually verifying each against its cited source before publication.

Common mistake

Fact-checking only the most prominent claims in a document while leaving smaller supporting claims unverified, where errors are just as capable of misleading a reader.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Hallucination Detection for the general technique this specializes

Citation validation confirms that a cited source actually exists and actually supports the specific claim attributed to it — catching a distinct failure mode from fact checking: fabricated or misattributed citations, where the cited source itself doesn't say what's claimed.

Why it matters

A confident-sounding citation to a real-looking source is one of the most convincing forms of hallucination (Level 5) — validating that the source exists and genuinely supports the claim is a distinct, necessary check beyond checking the claim's plausibility alone.

Core concepts

  • Source existence verification
  • Claim-to-source support verification (not just existence)
  • Fabricated citation detection

Real-world example

Checking that a cited paper actually exists, and that the specific finding attributed to it appears in that paper, not just a plausible-sounding but unrelated result.

Common mistake

Checking only that a citation "looks real" (proper formatting, plausible title) without verifying the source actually exists and says what's claimed.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Hallucination Detection for the broader pattern citation fabrication falls under

Paper summarization condenses a research source into its key claims, methods, and findings — applying Level 2's compression concept to individual sources so a literature review loop can work with concise representations instead of full texts.

Why it matters

Effective summarization here means preserving the specific details (sample sizes, effect sizes, methodology limitations) that later verification steps will need — over-compressing loses exactly the detail fact-checking depends on.

Core concepts

  • Preserving claims, methods, and limitations, not just conclusions
  • Summarization detail level vs. downstream verification needs
  • Structured extraction (claim, evidence, confidence) vs. prose summary

Real-world example

Summarizing a study's finding along with its sample size and stated limitations, not just its headline conclusion, so later verification can properly weigh its strength.

Common mistake

Summarizing away a study's caveats or limitations, producing a stronger-sounding claim than the source actually supports — directly connects to Level 2's over-compression risk.

Further reading

  • See Level 2 — Compression for the general technique this specializes

Knowledge synthesis combines findings from multiple sources into a coherent overall picture — resolving agreements, disagreements, and gaps between sources — applying Level 2's graph-of-thoughts aggregation concept to research findings specifically.

Why it matters

Individually-verified facts don't automatically add up to useful understanding — synthesis is the step that identifies where sources agree, where they genuinely conflict, and what remains an open question.

Core concepts

  • Cross-source agreement and disagreement resolution
  • Gap identification (what no source addresses)
  • Synthesis as aggregation (Level 2 — Graph Prompting)

Real-world example

Noting that three sources agree on a treatment's general effectiveness but disagree on optimal dosage, and explicitly flagging the dosage question as unresolved rather than picking one source's number silently.

Common mistake

Silently resolving disagreement between sources by picking one without flagging the conflict, presenting contested findings as settled consensus.

Further reading

  • Meta-analysis methodology literature on synthesizing findings across studies

Research automation composes this level's full stack — literature review, hypothesis generation, evidence collection, verification, synthesis — into an end-to-end research agent, typically with human checkpoints given how much harder research evaluation is than, say, coding's test suites.

Why it matters

Compared to Level 6's code agents, research agents face a structurally harder evaluation problem — there's rarely a deterministic check for "is this conclusion correct" — which is exactly why human-in-the-loop gating matters more here than in coding loops.

Core concepts

  • End-to-end composition of the research-loop stack
  • Human checkpoints given weaker automatic evaluation
  • Contrast with coding agents' stronger evaluation signal (Level 6)

Real-world example

A research agent that autonomously runs literature review and evidence collection, but presents its synthesized conclusion to a human for approval before it's treated as final.

Common mistake

Applying the same autonomy level used successfully for code agents to research agents, underestimating how much harder research's evaluation problem is than coding's.

Further reading

  • See Level 6 — Code Agents for a contrasting domain with stronger automatic evaluation
Level 8

Enterprise Loop Engineering

Everything needed to run loop-based systems reliably at scale, in production, with real users and real consequences — including the runtime, orchestration, durability, observability, security, computer-use, browser automation, environment control, governance, and resource controls that turn agent loops into operational systems. This layer also treats every execution trajectory as measurable infrastructure, with trace semantics, online/offline evaluation, failure attribution, regression detection, safety auditing, and continuous feedback into the loop.

Topics: 194 Est. time: ~16 hrs Prerequisites: Level 3, Level 5

Build a miniature multi-agent control plane that centrally governs identity, policy, registry, admission, routing, evaluation gates, SLOs, cost, observability, deployment, and incident response.

Why this project exists

This is the transition from “agent application” to “agent platform.” The project proves that you can operate many autonomous workloads with shared controls rather than hand-configuring each agent.

Builds on the previous level

Promotes L7 security controls into platform primitives and manages L3–L6 agents as registered workloads.

Architecture flow: Developer / User → Control Plane → Identity + Policy → Scheduler / Router → Agent Fleet → Telemetry / Eval / Incident → feedback to the next iteration

How to read the architecture

Left-to-right is the execution path. The dashed return path is the evidence/feedback path. Every box should have a testable contract; every boundary should emit evidence that can be replayed.

Skills this project proves

  • control-plane architecture
  • agent registry
  • identity propagation
  • policy-as-code
  • admission control
  • model/tool routing
  • fleet lifecycle
  • evaluation gates
  • SLOs/SLIs
  • cost attribution
  • incident automation
  • deployment governance

Recommended implementation stack

Kubernetes or Docker Compose, FastAPI, Postgres, Redis/queue, OTel, policy engine, CI/CD, container registry

Build sequence

1 · Register

Create agent/workload records with owner, version, capabilities, identity, risk tier, and lifecycle state.

2 · Govern

Implement admission policies, capability permissions, environment constraints, and promotion gates.

3 · Route

Add model/tool routing, scheduling, quotas, concurrency limits, and failure isolation.

4 · Observe

Collect traces, SLO metrics, evaluation results, cost attribution, and policy decisions.

5 · Operate

Implement rollback, quarantine, incident response, kill switches, and audit export.

6 · Package

Publish control-plane architecture, API spec, SLO dashboard, incident walkthrough, and deployment manifests.

Definition of done

  • Multiple agents share the same control plane.
  • Identity and policy are enforced centrally.
  • New versions cannot bypass evaluation/admission gates.
  • SLOs and cost are visible per agent/workflow.
  • An incident can quarantine a workload without destroying evidence.
  • A deployment can be rolled back reproducibly.

Portfolio evidence pack

  • platform architecture
  • API spec
  • policy repo
  • SLO dashboard
  • cost report
  • deployment manifests
  • incident runbook
  • demo

Public artifact

`agent-control-plane`: local/cloud-deployable control plane governing a small agent fleet with policy, eval, SLO, and incident controls.

Project-specific failure to avoid

A dashboard over a collection of agents with no central enforcement, identity, admission, lifecycle, or rollback authority.

Market research basis · 2026

2026 enterprise research points to identity, governance, centralized enforcement, monitoring, accountability, and production operations as major gaps in agent fleets.

Portfolio handoff

L9 composes the entire stack into one autonomous platform and adds institutional improvement.

A production agent is one running against real users and real consequences, not a development or evaluation environment — the gap between "the loop works on my benchmark" and "the loop works safely at scale, indefinitely, for people who didn't choose to be a test case" is what this whole level addresses.

Why it matters

Nearly every earlier topic behaves differently at production scale: rare edge cases that never appeared in a small test set happen constantly at volume, and failures affect real people rather than a benchmark score.

Core concepts

  • Scale-dependent failure modes (rare cases become common)
  • Real consequences vs. benchmark scores
  • The development-to-production gap as a distinct engineering problem

Real-world example

An edge case that occurred in 1 out of 10,000 test cases during evaluation happening dozens of times a day once the system serves millions of real requests.

Common mistake

Treating strong benchmark performance as sufficient evidence of production readiness, without the monitoring, fallback, and safety infrastructure this level covers.

Further reading

  • Site-reliability-engineering literature on the development-to-production gap

Monitoring is the production implementation of Level 5's performance-monitoring preview: continuously tracking key signals (quality scores, error rates, cost, latency) across all running loops, with alerting when something crosses a threshold.

Why it matters

A supervisor agent (Level 3) needs monitoring data to act on — without it, the supervisor role has no signal to base interventions on, and issues are discovered only when users report them.

Core concepts

  • Key metrics tracked continuously (quality, errors, cost, latency)
  • Alerting thresholds and escalation
  • Dashboards for human operators

Real-world example

A dashboard showing real-time error rate across all running agent loops, with an automatic alert firing if the rate exceeds 2% for more than five minutes.

Common mistake

Monitoring only technical metrics (uptime, latency) while ignoring quality metrics, missing a system that's "up" but silently producing degraded output.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Performance Monitoring for the evaluation concept this scales up

Logging records what happened during each loop iteration — inputs, outputs, decisions, errors — as a durable record that can be reviewed after the fact, distinct from monitoring's real-time aggregate view.

Why it matters

When monitoring surfaces an anomaly, logs are what let you actually investigate why it happened — without detailed logs, an alert tells you something's wrong but not what or why.

Core concepts

  • What to log (inputs, outputs, decisions, errors, timing)
  • Log retention and searchability
  • Structured logging vs. free-text logs

Real-world example

Reconstructing exactly why an agent made a specific decision at 3am by reviewing its logged reasoning trace for that iteration.

Common mistake

Logging free-text summaries that are hard to search or aggregate at scale, instead of structured, queryable log entries.

Further reading

  • Structured-logging best practices from observability platform documentation

Tracing follows a single request's full path through a multi-agent system — which agent handled it, which tools were called, how long each step took — reconstructing the entire execution flow, especially valuable for the multi-agent architectures in Level 3.

Why it matters

In a system with coordinators, workers, reviewers, and handoffs (Level 3), a single log line from one agent doesn't tell you the full story — tracing stitches together the entire journey of one request across every agent it touched.

Core concepts

  • Request-level trace ID linking all related log entries
  • Per-step timing within a trace
  • Trace visualization across multi-agent handoffs

Real-world example

Following one customer request's trace through a routing agent, a specialized billing agent, and a tool agent, seeing exactly how long each step took.

Common mistake

Logging each agent's activity independently without a shared trace ID linking them, making it impossible to reconstruct the full path of any single request after the fact.

Further reading

  • OpenAI's and other frameworks' documentation on agent tracing (see also Level 3 — OpenAI Agents Concepts)

Observability is the umbrella property that monitoring, logging, and tracing together provide: the ability to ask new questions about a running system's behavior after the fact, without having to have predicted that exact question in advance.

Why it matters

You can't predict every question you'll need to ask about a production incident in advance — good observability means the data to answer an unanticipated question is already there, rather than needing to add logging after the fact.

Core concepts

  • Observability as monitoring + logging + tracing combined
  • Answering unanticipated questions vs. pre-built dashboards
  • Observability as a design property, not a bolt-on feature

Real-world example

Answering "which specific tool call caused this cost spike last Tuesday" after the fact, using existing traces and logs, without having built a dashboard for that exact question in advance.

Common mistake

Building only pre-defined dashboards for anticipated questions, discovering during an actual incident that the needed data was never captured.

Further reading

  • Observability engineering literature (e.g., "Observability Engineering" by Majors, Fong-Jones & Miranda)

Incident response is the defined process for what happens when monitoring detects a serious problem — who's alerted, how the system is stabilized (often via the fallback systems covered next), and how the incident is documented afterward for future prevention.

Why it matters

Detecting a problem (monitoring) is only useful if there's a clear process for responding to it — without one, incidents get discovered but not necessarily addressed quickly or consistently.

Core concepts

  • Alert escalation and on-call ownership
  • Stabilization actions (fallback, rollback, kill switch)
  • Post-incident review and documentation

Real-world example

A defined process where a critical quality-drop alert pages an on-call engineer, who can trigger an immediate rollback to a previous known-good prompt version.

Common mistake

Having monitoring and alerting but no defined response process, so a fired alert doesn't reliably translate into timely action.

Further reading

  • Site-reliability-engineering literature on incident response and postmortem practices

Fallback systems are the production-scale implementation of Level 2's failure-handling concept: a predefined, simpler, more reliable behavior a system switches to when the primary loop fails or exceeds its budget — a cached answer, a simpler model, or a direct human handoff.

Why it matters

At production scale, some fraction of requests will hit the primary loop's failure conditions no matter how well-designed it is — a good fallback determines whether that failure is invisible to the user or a broken experience.

Core concepts

  • Graceful degradation vs. hard failure
  • Fallback triggers (timeout, error, budget exhaustion)
  • Fallback quality relative to primary-path quality

Real-world example

A complex multi-step agent falling back to a simpler, single-call response when it exceeds its time budget, rather than returning an error to the user.

Common mistake

Building a sophisticated primary loop with no fallback at all, so any failure in the primary path becomes a visible, user-facing failure with no graceful degradation.

Further reading

  • See Level 2 — Failure Handling for the general pattern this scales to production

Guardrails are input/output checks that run alongside a loop — not inside its main reasoning path — to catch unsafe, off-scope, or policy-violating behavior, the production-scale implementation of Level 3's OpenAI-Agents-Concepts preview.

Why it matters

Running guardrails as a separate parallel process, rather than folding safety checks into the main prompt, means a guardrail failure is independent of whatever's currently wrong with the main loop's reasoning.

Core concepts

  • Input guardrails (validate before processing) vs. output guardrails (validate before returning)
  • Parallel, independent checking vs. baked-into-the-prompt checking
  • Guardrail failure handling (block, flag, or degrade)

Real-world example

An output guardrail that independently scans every response for personally identifiable information before it's sent, regardless of what the main agent's reasoning concluded.

Common mistake

Relying solely on prompt instructions ("don't reveal PII") as the only safety mechanism, with no independent check that would catch a failure of that instruction.

Further reading

  • See Level 3 — OpenAI Agents Concepts for the guardrail pattern this scales to production

Security loops continuously test a production system against adversarial inputs — prompt injection attempts, jailbreaks, data exfiltration attempts through tool use — rather than checking security once before launch and assuming it holds.

Why it matters

Adversarial techniques evolve after launch; a security check done once pre-launch doesn't protect against new attack patterns discovered afterward — security needs its own ongoing loop, not a one-time gate.

Core concepts

  • Ongoing red-teaming vs. one-time pre-launch security review
  • Prompt injection and jailbreak detection
  • Tool-use security (preventing data exfiltration via tool agents)

Real-world example

Continuously testing a production agent with newly discovered jailbreak patterns from security research, not just the patterns known at launch time.

Common mistake

Treating a pre-launch security review as sufficient and permanent, missing new attack patterns that emerge after deployment.

Further reading

  • Published prompt-injection and jailbreak research from major AI labs and security researchers

Compliance is meeting the specific regulatory and legal requirements that apply to a system's domain and jurisdiction — data protection rules, industry-specific regulations, audit-trail requirements — which loop design has to accommodate rather than treat as an afterthought.

Why it matters

Compliance requirements often dictate specific loop design choices directly — a data-retention rule affects Level 4's memory-pruning policy; an audit requirement affects Level 8's logging design — so compliance needs to inform architecture early, not get bolted on later.

Core concepts

  • Domain- and jurisdiction-specific requirements
  • Compliance-driven constraints on memory, logging, and retention
  • Audit trails as a compliance artifact

Real-world example

A healthcare agent's memory-pruning policy (Level 4) designed around specific data-retention regulations rather than purely technical considerations.

Common mistake

Designing memory, logging, and retention policies purely for technical convenience, then discovering they violate a compliance requirement only during an audit.

Further reading

  • Domain-specific regulatory guidance (varies significantly by industry and jurisdiction)

Scaling addresses how a loop-based system behaves under growing request volume — whether individual loops can run concurrently without interfering, whether shared resources (memory stores, tool agents) become bottlenecks, and how cost and latency change as volume grows.

Why it matters

A loop design that works well at low volume can hit entirely different failure modes at high volume — a shared memory store (Level 4) that was fast with ten concurrent agents may become a bottleneck with ten thousand.

Core concepts

  • Concurrent loop execution and resource contention
  • Shared-resource bottlenecks (memory, tools, rate limits)
  • Cost and latency scaling curves as volume grows

Real-world example

Discovering that a shared vector memory store's retrieval latency degrades noticeably once concurrent agent load crosses a certain threshold, and needing to shard or cache it.

Common mistake

Load-testing a loop design only at the volume it was developed under, missing bottlenecks that only appear at production scale.

Further reading

  • Distributed-systems literature on scaling shared-resource architectures

Cost management is Level 5's cost-optimization concept applied at the whole-system, ongoing level: tracking aggregate spend across every running loop, setting organization-wide budgets, and catching cost anomalies (a runaway loop, an unexpectedly expensive query pattern) before they become a large bill.

Why it matters

A single misbehaving loop (echoing the AutoGPT runaway problem from Level 3) can generate enormous unplanned cost very quickly at production scale — system-level cost management is the safety net that catches this before it's discovered on an invoice.

Core concepts

  • Aggregate cost tracking across all running loops
  • Organization-wide and per-team budgets
  • Automated cost-anomaly detection and circuit breakers

Real-world example

An automatic circuit breaker that pauses a specific agent type if its hourly spend suddenly spikes to ten times its normal baseline.

Common mistake

Relying on end-of-month billing review as the only cost signal, discovering a runaway loop's cost impact weeks after it started rather than within hours.

Further reading

  • See Level 5 — Cost Optimization for the per-loop concept this scales to system-wide management

Reliability is the measured consistency of a loop-based system delivering correct results within acceptable time and cost bounds — combining uptime, quality consistency, and predictable behavior under varying conditions into one engineering concern.

Why it matters

Reliability ties together nearly every other topic in this level — monitoring, fallbacks, guardrails, and scaling all exist in service of one goal: the system behaves predictably and correctly, consistently, not just on average.

Core concepts

  • Uptime and quality consistency together, not separately
  • Reliability targets (e.g., service-level objectives)
  • Reliability under varying load and edge-case conditions

Real-world example

Setting an explicit reliability target — "95% of requests receive a quality-verified response within 3 seconds" — and designing fallback and monitoring systems specifically to hit that target.

Common mistake

Measuring average performance instead of worst-case or tail-case performance, missing that a system averaging well can still fail badly and often for a meaningful minority of requests.

Further reading

  • Site-reliability-engineering literature on service-level objectives (SLOs)

An agent runtime is the execution substrate that turns an agent definition into a running system: it owns the run lifecycle, state transitions, tool dispatch, scheduling, limits, retries, handoffs, and control signals around model calls.

Why it matters

Without a distinct runtime layer, orchestration logic leaks into prompts and application code, making behavior difficult to observe, test, resume, and govern.

Core engineering concepts

  • Run lifecycle and execution boundaries
  • Agent, turn, tool, and workflow scopes
  • Runtime state versus model-visible context
  • Pluggable model and tool adapters
  • Execution policies and middleware
  • Cancellation and interruption propagation
  • Resource accounting and budgets
  • Telemetry hooks and trace propagation
  • Error domains and failure classification
  • Runtime API boundaries and versioning

Real-world build

Build a minimal runtime around an agent that records every turn, tool call, state transition, budget decision, and terminal condition as structured events.

Common failure mode

Treating the model API call as the runtime itself, leaving state, retries, policy, and orchestration scattered across unrelated application code.

Further reading

  • Agent runtime and orchestration documentation from current production agent frameworks
  • Distributed-systems literature on schedulers, concurrency, queues, and failure handling

Run lifecycle management defines how an agent execution starts, advances through turns, pauses, fails, resumes, and reaches a terminal state. A runtime should make each transition explicit rather than hiding it inside an opaque call stack.

Why it matters

Long-running and multi-agent systems need predictable boundaries for setup, model invocation, tool execution, handoffs, interruption, and completion so operators can reason about what the system is doing.

Core engineering concepts

  • Run creation and initialization
  • Turn boundaries and iteration counters
  • Pre-run and post-run hooks
  • Terminal versus non-terminal outcomes
  • Pending tool and approval states
  • Timeout and deadline propagation
  • Cancellation tokens and cooperative stop
  • Resume semantics after interruption
  • Run metadata and correlation IDs
  • Finalization and cleanup guarantees

Real-world build

Implement a runner that exposes a state timeline for a research task and can stop after any turn, report its status, and continue from the recorded execution state.

Common failure mode

Representing the entire run as one uninterruptible function call, which makes cancellation, retries, and debugging brittle.

Further reading

  • Agent runtime and orchestration documentation from current production agent frameworks
  • Distributed-systems literature on schedulers, concurrency, queues, and failure handling

State-machine execution models an agent workflow as explicit states and transitions instead of relying solely on implicit conversational flow. The state machine defines what can happen next, under what conditions, and what transitions are legal.

Why it matters

Explicit transition logic prevents invalid jumps, makes workflows testable, and gives durable execution and observability a concrete model to record and replay.

Core engineering concepts

  • States and transition functions
  • Guards and transition predicates
  • Entry and exit actions
  • Terminal and error states
  • Nested and hierarchical states
  • State invariants
  • Event-driven transitions
  • Persisted execution state
  • Illegal-transition handling
  • Deterministic transition evaluation

Real-world build

Model a coding workflow as SPECIFIED → PLANNING → EDITING → TESTING → REVIEW → DONE/ROLLBACK and reject transitions that violate the workflow contract.

Common failure mode

Using a giant conditional chain with hidden side effects instead of explicit state and transition boundaries.

Further reading

  • Agent runtime and orchestration documentation from current production agent frameworks
  • Distributed-systems literature on schedulers, concurrency, queues, and failure handling

Agent schedulers decide when work executes, while work queues decouple task production from task execution. Together they let agent systems coordinate asynchronous tool calls, delegated subtasks, retries, priorities, and delayed work.

Why it matters

Once multiple agents or long-running tasks exist, synchronous call-and-return execution becomes a bottleneck. Scheduling turns agent execution into controllable workload management.

Core engineering concepts

  • FIFO, priority, weighted, and deadline scheduling
  • Queue partitioning and routing
  • Backpressure and admission control
  • Worker pools and capacity limits
  • Delayed and scheduled jobs
  • Fairness across tenants or tasks
  • Queue visibility timeouts
  • Retry queues and dead-letter queues
  • Duplicate delivery handling
  • Queue depth and scheduler telemetry

Real-world build

Build a queue-backed agent worker system that prioritizes urgent tasks, limits concurrent executions, retries transient failures, and sends poison jobs to a dead-letter queue.

Common failure mode

Adding concurrency without backpressure, causing queues and downstream tool providers to collapse under bursts.

Further reading

  • Agent runtime and orchestration documentation from current production agent frameworks
  • Distributed-systems literature on schedulers, concurrency, queues, and failure handling

Concurrency engineering determines which agent actions may run simultaneously, which must remain ordered, and how shared state is protected when multiple tasks execute at once.

Why it matters

Parallelism can cut latency dramatically, but uncontrolled concurrency creates races, duplicated side effects, token spikes, and provider-rate-limit failures.

Core engineering concepts

  • Independent versus dependent tasks
  • Fork/join patterns
  • Task groups and structured concurrency
  • Shared-state races

Text-only benchmarks cannot reveal the perception, interaction, environment, and recovery failures that dominate computer-use systems.

Governance is the organizational structure around who can approve deploying a new loop, who owns it once live, how changes get reviewed, and who's accountable when something goes wrong — the human decision-making process layered on top of the technical systems this level otherwise covers.

Why it matters

Even a technically excellent loop design can cause harm if deployed without appropriate review, or if no one is clearly accountable for its ongoing behavior — governance is the organizational counterpart to the supervisor agent role from Level 3.

Core concepts

  • Deployment approval processes
  • Ownership and accountability assignment
  • Change review for production loop modifications

Real-world example

A requirement that any new agent capable of autonomous financial transactions must be reviewed and approved by a specific committee before deployment.

Common mistake

Deploying increasingly autonomous loops without a correspondingly clear governance process, leaving no one accountable when the system's behavior needs to be questioned.

Further reading

  • AI governance frameworks published by major AI labs and standards bodies

Durable execution turns a best-effort agent loop into a workflow whose progress survives process crashes, machine loss, network interruptions, and long waits. Instead of treating the current invocation as the unit of truth, the system treats persisted execution state and recoverable progress as first-class artifacts.

Why it matters

A production agent can pause for hours while waiting for a user, external system, or scheduled event and later continue without restarting the entire task from scratch. Modern durable-execution systems expose checkpointing, retries, waits, callbacks, and replay as explicit primitives.

Core concepts

  • Persisted progress rather than invocation-local progress
  • Durable steps and operation boundaries
  • Long-running executions that outlive worker processes
  • External events and human waits
  • Recovery semantics as part of application design
  • Execution history as a source of truth
  • Durability vs. stateless request/response execution
  • Failure recovery without losing task progress
  • Lifecycle management for incomplete and completed executions
  • Durability as a prerequisite for reliable long-horizon agents

Real-world example

A research agent pauses after collecting evidence, waits for an external review signal, and resumes at the next unresolved step rather than repeating the entire literature search.

Common mistake

Calling an agent workflow durable merely because its database is persistent. Persistence of business data is not the same thing as durable execution state.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution SDK documentation — checkpoint/replay model
  • Temporal documentation — crash-proof workflow execution

Checkpointing records enough execution state at well-defined boundaries that a workflow can resume from a known safe point. Good checkpoints balance recovery granularity against storage, serialization, replay, and operational cost.

Why it matters

Without checkpoints, a failure near the end of a long agent run can force an expensive restart and may repeat side effects. With checkpoints, the recovery point becomes explicit and measurable.

Core concepts

  • Checkpoint boundaries and state snapshots
  • What belongs inside durable state
  • Checkpoint size and serialization cost
  • Frequency vs. recovery granularity
  • Checkpoint retention and cleanup
  • Externalizing large payloads and storing references
  • Parent vs. child workflow state
  • Versioning checkpoint schemas
  • Checkpoint corruption and recovery
  • Observability of checkpoint creation and restore

Real-world example

A coding agent checkpoints after repository inspection, planning, each validated patch, and a successful test stage so a worker crash does not erase the work already verified.

Common mistake

Persisting enormous model contexts or raw tool payloads into every checkpoint, turning recovery metadata into a storage and replay bottleneck.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution state-management guidance
  • Durable workflow checkpointing patterns

Replay reconstructs workflow progress from recorded execution history. On recovery, previously completed durable operations can return their recorded results while the orchestration logic advances toward work that has not yet completed.

Why it matters

Replay is what makes checkpoint-based recovery practical, but it imposes strict rules on what execution code is allowed to do outside durable operations.

Core concepts

  • Execution-history replay
  • Recorded step results
  • Skipping already-completed durable operations
  • Replay boundaries
  • History growth and compaction
  • Replay cost
  • Replay-driven debugging
  • Mismatch detection
  • Workflow history inspection
  • Recovery testing through forced replay

Real-world example

A workflow restarts after a worker crash, replays prior tool results from its execution history, and continues from the first unfinished operation without repeating the completed external calls.

Common mistake

Assuming replay means simply rerunning the same code from the beginning without considering which operations would create duplicate effects.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution replay documentation
  • Temporal workflow replay documentation

Durable orchestration code must make consistent control-flow decisions during replay. Non-deterministic behavior such as wall-clock reads, random values, uncontrolled external I/O, or mutable process-local state can cause replay to diverge from the recorded execution history.

Why it matters

Determinism is the hidden contract behind reliable replay. If the workflow takes a different branch after recovery, the persisted history can no longer safely describe the current execution path.

Core concepts

  • Deterministic orchestration
  • Pure control-flow logic
  • Time and randomness as nondeterministic inputs
  • External I/O isolation
  • Replay-safe identifiers
  • Deterministic branching
  • Workflow code evolution
  • Versioning around changed control flow
  • Replay mismatch detection
  • Testing deterministic recovery paths

Real-world example

A durable agent obtains timestamps and random identifiers inside explicit durable operations so replay receives the same recorded values instead of generating different ones.

Common mistake

Calling time, randomness, or external APIs directly from replay-sensitive orchestration code and assuming retries will magically make it safe.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution determinism guidance

Idempotency makes repeating a workflow step safe by ensuring the externally visible effect does not multiply when retries or replay cause an operation to run more than once.

Why it matters

Checkpointing without idempotency can turn recovery into corruption: an agent may resend an email, charge an account twice, create duplicate records, or submit duplicate jobs.

Core concepts

  • Idempotency keys
  • Conditional writes
  • Deduplication tokens
  • Exactly-once illusion vs practical semantics
  • At-least-once execution
  • At-most-once execution
  • Idempotent database mutations
  • External API idempotency
  • Side-effect classification
  • Designing retry-safe tool calls

Real-world example

A payment-capable agent generates an idempotency key for a payment attempt so a retry after a network timeout cannot create a second charge.

Common mistake

Assuming a timeout means the action did not happen. A client can lose the response after the external system has already committed the side effect.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution idempotency guidance

Retries are controlled re-executions of failed operations. Reliable agent systems distinguish transient failures from permanent failures and apply bounded, observable retry policies instead of blindly repeating every error.

Why it matters

Agent workflows are exposed to rate limits, network failures, model provider errors, expired credentials, tool outages, and temporary infrastructure faults. Retry policy determines whether the loop recovers gracefully or creates a retry storm.

Core concepts

  • Transient vs permanent failure classification
  • Exponential backoff
  • Jitter
  • Maximum attempts and total retry budgets
  • Per-error retry policies
  • Circuit breakers
  • Dead-letter handling
  • Retry observability
  • Idempotency as a prerequisite
  • Escalation after retry exhaustion

Real-world example

A model call receives a transient 429, waits with exponential backoff and jitter, retries within a cost budget, and escalates only after the retry policy is exhausted.

Common mistake

Retrying validation failures, authorization failures, or deterministic bugs as though they were transient outages.

Further reading

  • Temporal retry policy documentation
  • AWS Durable Execution retry guidance

Long-running agents often need to stop doing work while waiting for something outside the workflow: a human approval, webhook, timer, batch job, or external service. Durable waits and signals let execution suspend without losing its state.

Why it matters

This converts an agent from a request/response program into a persistent process that can survive hours, days, or longer between meaningful events.

Core concepts

  • Timer-based waits
  • External signals
  • Human approval callbacks
  • Webhook-triggered continuation
  • Waiting without consuming compute
  • Timeout policies
  • Cancellation during waits
  • Race conditions between signals and timeouts
  • Resuming from durable state
  • Event correlation and identity

Real-world example

An enterprise agent submits a procurement request, enters a durable wait, and resumes automatically when an approval callback arrives the next morning.

Common mistake

Keeping a worker process alive while waiting for a human or external event, wasting resources and making failure recovery fragile.

Further reading

  • AWS Durable Execution wait/callback primitives
  • Temporal signals and timers

Operationally mature agents need explicit control over running executions: pause them, cancel them, terminate dangerous work, or resume safely after intervention. These controls are distinct from ordinary failure recovery.

Why it matters

A production supervisor may need to stop an agent because requirements changed, a security incident was detected, a budget was exceeded, or human review is required.

Core concepts

  • Cooperative cancellation
  • Hard termination
  • Pause/resume semantics
  • Cancellation propagation
  • Cleanup on cancellation
  • Human-triggered interruption
  • Partial progress after cancellation
  • Resumption policies
  • Cancellation audit trails
  • Safe termination of tool calls

Real-world example

A supervisor pauses an agent before a high-impact external action, requests human review, then resumes from the last safe checkpoint after approval.

Common mistake

Treating cancellation as equivalent to deleting the execution state, making safe resume impossible.

Further reading

  • Durable workflow cancellation and interruption patterns

Not every distributed action can be rolled back with a database transaction. Compensation uses explicit corrective actions to recover from partially completed multi-step workflows when later steps fail.

Why it matters

Agent workflows can cross APIs, databases, ticketing systems, cloud services, and human processes. A robust recovery strategy must reason about partial completion rather than pretending all actions are atomic.

Core concepts

  • Forward progress vs compensation
  • Compensating actions
  • Saga-style workflows
  • Irreversible actions
  • Compensation ordering
  • Partial failure states
  • Manual remediation
  • Consistency across services
  • Compensation idempotency
  • Auditability of recovery actions

Real-world example

An onboarding agent creates an account, provisions access, and opens tickets; if provisioning fails, it executes a defined compensation path to revoke already-granted access and mark the onboarding state for review.

Common mistake

Writing a generic 'undo everything' routine for side effects that are not truly reversible.

Further reading

  • Saga pattern literature
  • Distributed workflow compensation patterns

Stateful agents require an explicit model of what is known, what has been attempted, what has succeeded, what is pending, and what remains unresolved. Execution state is broader than conversational memory: it represents the current lifecycle of work.

Why it matters

Separating task state from conversational context prevents agents from inferring critical workflow state from prose alone. Explicit state makes recovery, auditing, and debugging far more reliable.

Core concepts

  • Workflow state vs memory
  • State machines for agent execution
  • Pending/in-flight/completed states
  • State transition invariants
  • Derived vs authoritative state
  • State ownership
  • State versioning
  • State serialization
  • State validation
  • Cross-step state consistency

Real-world example

A research workflow stores explicit fields such as current hypothesis, evidence status, reviewer decision, pending tool action, and completion criteria instead of encoding all of that solely in chat history.

Common mistake

Treating the conversation transcript as the authoritative workflow state when it may omit, contradict, or obscure critical lifecycle information.

Further reading

  • State-machine and durable-workflow design literature

Durable workflows must be tested under the failures that ordinary unit tests rarely model: crashes between side effects, repeated delivery, interrupted waits, replay, timeouts, partial tool failures, and corrupted or incompatible state.

Why it matters

The system is supposed to remain correct precisely when things go wrong. Testing only the happy path proves almost none of the durability guarantees you care about.

Core concepts

  • Replay testing
  • Crash injection at step boundaries
  • Duplicate delivery testing
  • Retry exhaustion
  • Interrupted waits
  • Cancellation tests
  • State migration tests
  • Determinism tests
  • Idempotency verification
  • Recovery-time and replay-cost benchmarks

Real-world example

A CI suite deliberately interrupts an agent immediately before and after an external tool call, then verifies that recovery produces the correct final state without duplicated side effects.

Common mistake

Testing only successful end-to-end runs and declaring the workflow reliable because it 'usually works.'

Further reading

  • AWS durable execution test-runner guidance
  • Failure-injection and workflow reliability testing

Durable agents live longer than a single deployment, so their persisted execution state must survive application-version changes. State schema evolution is the discipline of changing serialized workflow state without making old executions unrecoverable or causing replay to interpret data under the wrong structure.

Why it matters

A long-running agent may have checkpoints created by yesterday's code while today's deployment expects a different schema. Safe upgrades require explicit compatibility and migration strategies, not hope that the old state will deserialize correctly.

Core concepts

  • Backward-compatible state changes
  • Versioned workflow/state schemas
  • Lazy vs. eager state migration
  • Defaulting newly introduced fields
  • Renaming and splitting persisted fields
  • Migration of in-flight executions
  • Replay compatibility across deployments
  • Dual-read and dual-write migration strategies
  • Rollback-safe schema design
  • Testing old checkpoints against new code

Real-world example

A research agent originally stores evidence as a plain list; a later release introduces typed evidence records with provenance and confidence. The runtime migrates old checkpoints on read while keeping the workflow resumable during the deployment transition.

Common mistake

Deploying a state-model change that works for brand-new executions but silently breaks already-running workflows that still contain older checkpoint data.

Further reading

  • Durable workflow versioning and replay-compatibility patterns
  • Schema migration patterns for long-lived distributed state

Human approvals are specific checkpoints within a running loop where execution pauses for explicit human sign-off before continuing — the concrete mechanism implementing Level 3's "human-in-the-loop vs. fully autonomous" design question at production scale.

Why it matters

Deciding exactly where to place approval checkpoints — every action, only irreversible ones, only above a cost threshold — is one of the highest-leverage design decisions in a production loop, directly trading off speed against risk.

Core concepts

  • Checkpoint placement (which actions require approval)
  • Reversible vs. irreversible actions as an approval criterion
  • Approval latency vs. autonomy trade-off

Real-world example

An agent requiring human approval before sending an external email or making a payment, but running fully autonomously for internal, reversible actions like drafting or searching.

Common mistake

Requiring approval for every single action regardless of reversibility or cost, which makes the system too slow to be useful and trains operators to rubber-stamp approvals without real scrutiny.

Further reading

  • See Level 3 — coordinator/supervisor agent roles for where approval checkpoints typically sit in a multi-agent system
